<section class="level1" data-number="1" id="executive-summary">
<h1 data-number="1"><span class="header-section-number">1</span> Executive summary</h1>
<p>The last full EBS pollock assessment was completed in 2024 <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2024safe">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2024safe" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2024</a>)</span>. A catch report was prepared in 2025 <span class="citation" data-cites="afsc2025pollockcatch">(<a href="#ref-afsc2025pollockcatch" role="doc-biblioref">Alaska Fisheries Science Center, National Marine Fisheries Service 2025</a>)</span>. Changes in this assessment are described relative to 2024.</p>
<p>This executive summary presents Model 26.0 (Rceattle), the base model for this assessment and its Tier 3 harvest recommendations. Model 23.0 (ADMB), accepted in 2024, provides the comparison with the previous assessment.</p>
<section class="level2" data-number="1.1" id="changes-in-assessment-inputs"><h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="changes-in-assessment-inputs" data-number="1.1"><span class="header-section-number">1.1</span> Changes in assessment inputs</h2><p>Catch, fishery age compositions, survey indices and age compositions, and weight-at-age schedules have been updated since 2024. <a href="#changes-inputs-detail">Section 2.1.1</a> describes the years, sources and data treatments.</p></section>
<section class="level2" data-number="1.2" id="changes-in-assessment-methods"><h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="changes-in-assessment-methods" data-number="1.2"><span class="header-section-number">1.2</span> Changes in assessment methods</h2><p>Model 26.0 implements the age-structured assessment in Rceattle and uses weight-at-age schedules estimated by a separate random-effects model. <a href="#changes-methods-detail">Section 2.1.2</a> describes these changes from Model 23.0.</p></section>
<section class="level2" data-number="1.3" id="summary-of-results">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="summary-of-results" data-number="1.3"><span class="header-section-number">1.3</span> Summary of results</h2>
<p>Estimated total biomass in 2026 is 12.162 million t (approximate 95% log-scale Wald confidence interval 9.534–15.515 million t). Female spawning biomass (SSB) is 3.057 million t (2.489–3.754 million t, using the same interval method). The largest fishing mortality rate among ages is 0.3 per year.</p>
<p>Scenario 2, the expected-catch projection scenario, assumes catches of 1.375 million t in each of 2027 and 2028, equal to the specified 2027 annual TAC. The projections use mean 2023–2025 fishery selectivity, fixed biological inputs and recruitment equal to the fitted 1978–2023 mean (<a href="#sec-projections">Section 7</a>).</p>
<p>The <a href="#advice-model260">advice table</a> compares the 2025–2026 recommendations from the 2024 assessment with this assessment’s 2027–2028 recommendations. Projected female spawning biomass and age 3+ biomass use Scenario 2 with the assumed catches above.</p>
<p>The final specifications for 2026 and 2027, issued in the absence of a 2025 stock assessment, specified the Bering Sea subarea pollock OFL at 2,496,000 t and ABC at 2,036,000 t; specified annual TAC is 1,375,000 t. These are the adopted specifications, separate from the recommendations from this assessment.</p>
<p>The stock is above MSST in 2026 and is not approaching an overfished condition (<a href="#sec-status-determination">Section 9</a>). All risk categories are Level 1, supporting maximum ABC (<a href="#sec-risk-table-abc">Section 8</a>).</p>

<section class="level2" data-number="1.4" id="sec-responses">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-responses" data-number="1.4"><span class="header-section-number">1.4</span> SSC and Plan Team requests</h2>
<p>The September 2026 Plan Team requested the following work:</p>
<ul>
<li>Present Model 26.0 for management use and Model 23.0 for continuity; both are compared in this assessment.</li>
<li>Examine age-1 BTS selectivity and the influence of BTS variability on retrospective patterns. Additional selectivity and data-influence tests are outside the scope of this assessment.</li>
<li>Extend the simulation self-test and examine retrospective patterns in time-varying selectivity. The completed simulation experiment and its limitations are described in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-model260-selftest">Section 6.3.1</a>.</li>
<li>Present retrospective results for Models 23.0 and 26.0 side by side. Matched runs were completed and compared; both models showed similar spawning-biomass retrospective patterns (<a href="#sec-prior-ssc">Appendix A</a>).</li>
<li>Document age-composition weighting and evaluate residual patterns. Selected sample sizes, one-step-ahead residuals and Francis comparisons are presented in the assessment.</li>
<li>Continue development of the Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile; we developed a draft using AI to compile and coordinate information from disparate sources (<a href="#sec-esp-2026-appendix">Appendix B</a>).</li>
</ul>
<p>Earlier SSC requests address model development, uncertainty, survey treatment and composition weighting. The individual requests and responses are presented in <a href="#sec-prior-ssc">Appendix A</a>.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="2" id="introduction">
<h1 data-number="2"><span class="header-section-number">2</span> Introduction</h1>
<section class="level2" data-number="2.1" id="general">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="general" data-number="2.1"><span class="header-section-number">2.1</span> General</h2>
<p>Walleye pollock (<em>Gadus chalcogrammus</em>; hereafter referred to as pollock) are broadly distributed throughout the North Pacific with the largest concentrations found in the eastern Bering Sea (EBS). Also known as Alaska pollock, this species continues to play important roles ecologically and economically.</p><section class="level3" data-number="2.1.1" id="changes-inputs-detail"><h3 data-number="2.1.1"><span class="header-section-number">2.1.1</span> Changes in assessment inputs</h3>
<p>The 2026 assessment updates the accepted December 2024 assessment; the 2025 document was a catch report. Updated inputs include annual catches from 1991 onward, fishery age compositions for 2024–2025, BTS indices and age compositions for 2025–2026, the 2026 ATS index and provisional age composition, and AVO indices through 2026. Historical BTS estimates were also revised. Spatiotemporal survey estimation continues the approach adopted in 2024; the current biomass-index and abundance-at-age products use sdmTMB (<span class="citation" data-cites="anderson2025sdmtmb"><a href="#ref-anderson2025sdmtmb" role="doc-biblioref">Anderson et al. 2025</a></span>) and tinyVAST (<span class="citation" data-cites="thorson2025tinyvast"><a href="#ref-thorson2025tinyvast" role="doc-biblioref">Thorson et al. 2025</a></span>), respectively.</p>
<p>The 2024–2025 fishery age compositions use year-specific FT-NIRS-to-traditional-microscopic-age conversions, with likelihood sample sizes of 578 and 530. The provisional 2026 ATS age composition applies the BTS age–length key to ATS lengths; FT-NIRS ages from the ATS samples are expected in 2027.</p>
<p>Fishery weight-at-age retains the fixed 1964–1990 schedule and annual observation means for 1991–2025. A separate random-effects model fitted to fishery and BTS weights through 2025 supplies 2026 predictions and 2027–2028 forecasts; its fit omits the 2026 BTS observations. Population weights use BTS means through 2026, including revised historical estimates. Spawning weights at ages 3–15+ use fitted 2024–2025 A-season weights and a 2026 projection, retaining the previous ages 1–2 schedule. <a href="#sec-data">Section 4</a> and <a href="#sec-ftnir-appendix">Appendix G</a> and <a href="#sec-bts-spatiotemporal-appendix">Appendix H</a> describe the data treatments and their uncertainty.</p></section>
<section class="level3" data-number="2.1.2" id="changes-methods-detail"><h3 data-number="2.1.2"><span class="header-section-number">2.1.2</span> Changes in assessment methods</h3>
<p>The main assessment-method change is the transition from the ADMB implementation of Model 23.0 to the Rceattle implementation of Model 26.0. Weight-at-age is estimated in a separate random-effects model and used as fixed schedules, whereas Model 23.0 estimates cohort and year effects within the assessment. Model 26.0 uncertainty therefore conditions on the estimated weights. Natural mortality and catchability assumptions retain the previous treatment. The configuration comparisons, diagnostics and sensitivities evaluate the effects of the data updates and implementation change (<a href="#sec-approach">Section 5</a>, <a href="#sec-results">Section 6</a> and <a href="#review-and-source-record">Appendix I</a>).</p></section></section>
<section class="level2" data-number="2.2" id="review-of-life-history">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="review-of-life-history" data-number="2.2"><span class="header-section-number">2.2</span> Review of Life History</h2>
<p>In the EBS, pollock generally spawn during March–May and in relatively localized regions during specific periods (<span class="citation" data-cites="bailey2000"><a href="#ref-bailey2000" role="doc-biblioref">Bailey 2000</a></span>). Generally spawning begins nearshore north of Unimak Island in March and April and later near the Pribilof Islands (<span class="citation" data-cites="bacheler2010">Bacheler et al. (<a href="#ref-bacheler2010" role="doc-biblioref">2010</a>)</span>). Females spawn in batches with up to 10 batches of eggs per female per year (during the peak spawning period). Eggs and larvae of EBS pollock are planktonic for a period of about 90 days and appear to be sensitive to environmental conditions. These conditions likely affect their dispersal into favorable areas (for subsequent separation from predators) and also affect general food requirements for over-wintering survival (<span class="citation" data-cites="gann2015">Gann et al. (<a href="#ref-gann2015" role="doc-biblioref">2015</a>)</span>, <span class="citation" data-cites="heintz2013">Heintz et al. (<a href="#ref-heintz2013" role="doc-biblioref">2013</a>)</span>, <span class="citation" data-cites="hunt2011">Hunt Jr. et al. (<a href="#ref-hunt2011" role="doc-biblioref">2011</a>)</span>, <span class="citation" data-cites="ciannelli2004">Ciannelli et al. (<a href="#ref-ciannelli2004" role="doc-biblioref">2004</a>)</span>). <span class="citation" data-cites="duffy2016">Duffy-Anderson et al. (<a href="#ref-duffy2016" role="doc-biblioref">2016</a>)</span> provide a review of the early life history of EBS pollock.</p>
<p>Throughout their range juvenile pollock feed on a variety of planktonic crustaceans, including calanoid copepods and euphausiids. In the EBS shelf region, one-year-old pollock are found throughout the water column, but also commonly occur in the NMFS bottom trawl survey. Ages 2 and 3 year old pollock are rarely caught in summer bottom trawl survey gear and are more common in the midwater zone as detected by mid-water acoustic trawl surveys. Younger pollock are generally found in the more northern parts of the survey area and appear to move to the southeast as they age (<span class="citation" data-cites="buckley2009">Buckley et al. (<a href="#ref-buckley2009" role="doc-biblioref">2009</a>)</span>). Euphausiids, principally <em>Thysanoessa inermis</em> and <em>T. raschii</em>, are among the most important prey items for pollock in the Bering Sea (<span class="citation" data-cites="livingston1991">Livingston (<a href="#ref-livingston1991" role="doc-biblioref">1991</a>)</span>; <span class="citation" data-cites="lang2000">Lang et al. (<a href="#ref-lang2000" role="doc-biblioref">2000</a>)</span>; <span class="citation" data-cites="brodeur2002">Brodeur et al. (<a href="#ref-brodeur2002" role="doc-biblioref">2002</a>)</span>; <span class="citation" data-cites="ciannelli2004">Ciannelli et al. (<a href="#ref-ciannelli2004" role="doc-biblioref">2004</a>)</span>; <span class="citation" data-cites="lang2005">Lang et al. (<a href="#ref-lang2005" role="doc-biblioref">2005</a>)</span>). Pollock diets become more piscivorous with age, and cannibalism has been commonly observed in this region. However, <span class="citation" data-cites="buckley2015">Buckley et al. (<a href="#ref-buckley2015" role="doc-biblioref">2015</a>)</span> showed that spatial patterns of pollock foraging, including cannibalism, vary with the size of the foraging pollock. For example, pollock in the northern shelf region between the 100 and 200 m isobaths (closest to the shelf break) tend to be more piscivorous than pollock in shallow nearshore areas.</p>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="2.3" id="sec-stock-structure-life-history">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-stock-structure-life-history" data-number="2.3"><span class="header-section-number">2.3</span> Stock structure</h2>
<p>Stock structure for EBS pollock was evaluated in <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2015">Ianelli et al. (<a href="#ref-ianelli2015" role="doc-biblioref">2015</a>)</span>. In that review past work on genetics (e.g., <span class="citation" data-cites="bailey1999">Bailey et al. (<a href="#ref-bailey1999" role="doc-biblioref">1999</a>)</span>, <span class="citation" data-cites="canino2005">Canino et al. (<a href="#ref-canino2005" role="doc-biblioref">2005</a>)</span>) provided insight on genetic differentiation. The investigation also compared synchrony in year-classes and growth patterns by region. Pollock samples from areas including Zhemchug Canyon, Japan, Prince William Sound, Bogoslof, Shelikof, and the northern Bering Sea were processed and results presented in <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2021">Ianelli et al. (<a href="#ref-ianelli2021" role="doc-biblioref">2021</a>)</span>. Genetics research at the AFSC <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2023a">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2023a" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2023</a>)</span> indicated that genetic groups mostly aligned with current stock-management delineations. The Aleutian Islands and Bogoslof stocks showed subtle differentiation from the Gulf of Alaska stocks.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="3" id="fishery-and-management-history">
<h1 data-number="3"><span class="header-section-number">3</span> Fishery and management history</h1>
<p>Directed foreign fishing began in 1964. US vessels entered the fishery in 1980, and it became fully domestic by 1988. The domestic observer program formally began in 1990; later monitoring developments include electronic monitoring on participating catcher vessels and biological sampling during offloading <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2024safe">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2024safe" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2024</a>)</span>. The directed fishery primarily uses pelagic trawl gear, with inshore, catcher/processor and mothership sectors. The historical catch and adopted harvest-limit series is continued through 2026 in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-catch-management-history">Table 1</a>.</p>
<p>Updated reported catches are 1,311,261 t in 2024 (2025 catch report) and 1,326,193 t in 2025 <span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2025inseason">(<a href="#ref-noaa2025inseason" role="doc-biblioref">National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Region 2026b</a>)</span>. The catch table reports two 2026 values: reported catch of 1,297,206 t through October 17 <span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2026cas">(<a href="#ref-noaa2026cas" role="doc-biblioref">National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Region 2026a</a>)</span> and the annual catch estimate of 1,312,504.58 t used in this assessment.</p>
<p>For 2026, the adopted ABC and OFL are 2,036,000 and 2,496,000 t. The Bering Sea subarea TAC increased from 1,375,000 to 1,389,500 t after inseason reallocations. The August allocations included 139,400 t for Community Development Quota (CDQ) directed fishing and 46,000 t for incidental catch. Bering Sea catch totals include CDQ directed catch and incidental catch, including incidental CDQ catch. Bogoslof and Aleutian Islands catches are reported separately <span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2026specifications noaa2026reallocation">(<a href="#ref-noaa2026specifications" role="doc-biblioref">National Marine Fisheries Service 2026a</a>, <a href="#ref-noaa2026reallocation" role="doc-biblioref">2026c</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>The directed pollock allowance is allocated 45% to the A season (January 20–June 10) and 55% to the B season (June 10–November 1). The non-CDQ allowance is divided among the inshore (50%), catcher/processor (40%) and mothership (10%) sectors. In the Steller sea lion conservation area, each sector may catch up to 28% of its annual directed allowance before noon April 1 <span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2026specifications">(<a href="#ref-noaa2026specifications" role="doc-biblioref">National Marine Fisheries Service 2026a</a>)</span>. The Winter Herring Savings Area (58–60° N, 172–175° W) is closed to directed pollock trawling, including CDQ fishing, from September 30, 2026, to March 1, 2027 <span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2026herringclosure">(<a href="#ref-noaa2026herringclosure" role="doc-biblioref">National Marine Fisheries Service 2026b</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Area restrictions, allocations, monitoring, and incentives are used to reduce prohibited species catch in the EBS pollock fishery. <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-management-measures">Table 2</a> summarizes major management changes. Industry cooperatives use rolling-hotspot closures to move fishing away from areas of high salmon bycatch. These voluntary programs began for chum salmon in 2001 and Chinook salmon in 2002. Amendment 84, implemented in 2007, allowed participating vessels to use approved intercooperative bycatch-reduction agreements in place of specified fixed salmon-area closures <span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2007am84 noaa2023salmonhistory">(<a href="#ref-noaa2007am84" role="doc-biblioref">National Marine Fisheries Service 2007</a>, <a href="#ref-noaa2023salmonhistory" role="doc-biblioref">2023</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Amendment 91 established Chinook salmon bycatch limits and incentives to reduce bycatch while allowing the pollock TAC to be harvested. Implemented in the 2011 fishery, it combined a 60,000-fish annual prohibited species catch (PSC) limit with incentive plan agreements and a 47,591-fish performance standard. A sector that exceeds its share of the standard in three of seven consecutive years receives a lower allocation in all subsequent years. Amendment 110, implemented in 2016, strengthened Chinook and chum avoidance and tied Chinook limits to salmon returns in western Alaska. When the State of Alaska’s index for the Kuskokwim, Unalakleet and Upper Yukon systems is 250,000 fish or less, the following year’s PSC limit and performance standard fall to 45,000 and 33,318 fish, respectively. The index first applied to the 2017 fishery <span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2010am91 noaa2016am110">(<a href="#ref-noaa2010am91" role="doc-biblioref">National Marine Fisheries Service 2010</a>, <a href="#ref-noaa2016am110" role="doc-biblioref">2016</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>NOAA Fisheries’ North Pacific Groundfish and Halibut Observer Program provides the salmon counts used to monitor PSC limits in the Bering Sea pollock fishery. Regulations require vessels to retain salmon until observers can count them at at-sea processors or during offloading. Catcher vessels carry an observer or an electronic monitoring (EM) system, and shoreside observers count salmon in deliveries <span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2025electronicmonitoringalaska">(<a href="#ref-noaa2025electronicmonitoringalaska" role="doc-biblioref">National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Regional Office 2025</a>)</span>. The Alaska Fisheries Science Center’s Genetics Program analyzes tissue samples collected by observers to identify the salmon stocks caught as bycatch. These stock-composition estimates help assess impacts on salmon populations and guide avoidance measures (<a href="https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/alaska/bycatch/chinook-salmon-bycatch-management-alaska">NOAA Fisheries salmon bycatch monitoring</a>). Genetic sampling of the 2015 Chinook bycatch is described by <span class="citation" data-cites="guthrie2017chinook2015">(<a href="#ref-guthrie2017chinook2015" role="doc-biblioref">Guthrie et al. 2017</a>)</span>.</p>
<section class="level2" data-number="3.1" id="sec-fishery-conditions">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-fishery-conditions" data-number="3.1"><span class="header-section-number">3.1</span> Fishery conditions</h2>
<p>The A-season fishery targets pre-spawning pollock and supports roe production. Fishing has historically concentrated north and west of Unimak Island and along the shelf toward the Pribilof Islands, with access affected by ice, weather and fish distribution. The summer–fall B-season fishery follows changes in fish availability across the shelf. Salmon-avoidance measures and vessel choices also influence where fishing occurs. Available observer data suggest good fishing conditions in the 2026 A season; later in the B season fishing moved farther north and pollock of desirable sizes were less available.</p>
<p>Catch by area and season is summarized in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-catch-area-season">Table 3</a>. The catch as of October 17, 2026, was 1,267,543 t: 604,041 t in the A season and 663,501 t in the B season.</p>
<p><a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-catch-retained-discarded">Table 4</a> summarizes annual retained and discarded catch. The 2026 total is 1,312,505 t, including 8,997 t discarded (0.7%).</p>
<p>Nominal pollock catch per tow-hour is generally higher in the A season than in the B season, with A-season peaks in 2019 and 2023 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-nominal-seasonal-cpue">Figure 1</a>). Species-specific patterns differ: A-season Chinook rates peak in 2006–2007, whereas the chum salmon series has its largest B-season rates in 2005 and 2017. Herring and sablefish each have a pronounced peak in 2020, in the A and B seasons respectively. These are nominal rates for available pollock-dominated EBS hauls, calculated from summed catch and valid tow-hours with panel-specific units. </p>
<p>Estimated catch numbers for both sexes decline to a trough in 2009, rise again during the 2010s and reach their largest annual totals in 2021 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-catch-numbers-sex-season">Figure 2</a>). B-season numbers generally exceed A-season numbers within each sex, and female annual catch numbers decline from 1,075.8 million fish in 2023 to 916.7 million in 2025, while male catch numbers decline from 1,218.9 million to 952.6 million. Catch numbers are expressed in thousands of fish. </p>
<p>The cumulative monthly depiction shows whether A-season fishing activity has shifted toward earlier or later months within the year. Cumulative catch through April stays near 40% of annual specified TAC over much of 2000–2017 and near 44% from 2018 onward (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-cumulative-catch-tac">Figure 3</a>). In 2026 the cumulative shares are 6.69%, 23.14%, 39.42% and 43.72% at the end of January, February, March and April, respectively. Monthly totals are based on weekly catch reports and the specified annual TAC before quota transfers. These observations cover the first four months of the year; the A season continues through June 10.</p>
<p>As expected, A-season roe production exceeds B-season production throughout the 2000–2026 series (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-roe-production">Figure 4</a>). A-season production peaks in 2006 and again in 2019, declines through 2021 and rises from 2022 to 2026. The latest A-season value is 19,092.9 t of roe. The 2025 B-season total is 1,795.8 t; the 2026 total of 406.4 t covers June–October and represents a partial-season estimate. </p>
<p>The broader BSAI fishery’s catch, vessel participation and market context are summarized in the <a href="#esp2026-economic-observations">ESP socioeconomic tables</a>. </p>
<section class="level3" data-number="3.1.1" id="recent-spatial-catch-patterns">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="recent-spatial-catch-patterns" data-number="3.1.1"><span class="header-section-number">3.1.1</span> Recent spatial catch patterns</h3>
<p>The seasonal maps compare 2024–2026 using the available catch-location records (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-spatial-catch-a">Figure 5</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-spatial-catch-b">Figure 6</a>). A-season maps cover January 20–June 9. B-season maps use June 10–September 18 in every year, matching the 2026 data cutoff. Vertical bar heights show catch tons. The rotated, elevated view separates neighboring columns. Each season uses a fixed vertical scale across its three years, with a 10,000-t reference column in each panel. The vertical scales differ between seasons.</p>
<p>A-season fishing remained concentrated on the southeastern shelf, with more catch extending westward in 2025. The share of available observed catch west of 170°W increased from 15% in 2024 to 39% in 2025, then returned to 15% in 2026. The catch-weighted mean latitude changed from 56.07°N to 56.43°N and 56.19°N, respectively. The 2026 pattern therefore shifted back toward the southeastern grounds relative to 2025.</p>
<p>The B-season distribution extended farther north and west in 2025–2026 than in 2024. The share of catch north of 58°N increased from 54% in 2024 to 75% in 2025 and 79% in 2026. The share west of 170°W rose from 76% to about 92% in both later years. Catch-weighted mean latitude was 57.66°N in 2024, 58.56°N in 2025 and 58.52°N in 2026. Thus, the recent northward shift persisted in 2026, while the catch-weighted mean longitude moved eastward relative to 2025, from 174.65°W to 173.26°W.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="3.1.2" id="fleet-dispersion">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="fleet-dispersion" data-number="3.1.2"><span class="header-section-number">3.1.2</span> Fleet dispersion</h3>
<p>Fleet dispersion describes how widely separated fishing locations are within a day (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-fleet-dispersion-current">Figure 7</a>). Following the 2024 assessment, we calculate the great-circle distance between each unique pair of tows made on the same day, separately for catcher-processors and observed catcher vessels. Distance sums and pair counts are then pooled by year and season. Days with more tow pairs contribute more to the seasonal average. Larger values indicate a more dispersed pattern of observed fishing locations; smaller values indicate greater concentration.</p>
<p>A-season dispersion increased from 47.8 nautical miles in 2024 to 68.8 in 2025, then declined to 36.5 in 2026. This change is consistent with the 2025 westward extension and the more concentrated southeastern pattern in 2026 shown in the catch maps. For B-season records through September 18 in each year, dispersion declined from 78.5 nautical miles in 2024 to 67.8 in 2025 and 56.5 in 2026. Thus, the observed B-season fishing locations became more concentrated even as much of the catch remained farther north than in 2024. A shift in fishing location and a change in spatial spread describe different aspects of fleet behavior.</p>
<p> Changes in the mix of observed vessels, bycatch avoidance and fishing conditions can influence this index, so it should be interpreted together with catch distribution and catch rates.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="3.1.3" id="seasonal-changes-in-fish-size">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="seasonal-changes-in-fish-size" data-number="3.1.3"><span class="header-section-number">3.1.3</span> Seasonal changes in fish size</h3>
<p>Mean fish weight is the pollock weight divided by the corresponding fish count. Weight-bin distributions show how the sizes encountered by the fishery change over time (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-seasonal-mean-weight">Figure 8</a>). </p>
<p>The dominant A-season mean-weight bin increased from 550 g in 2023 to 600 g in 2024–2025 and 700 g in 2026. For the B season, the dominant bin increased from 450 g in 2023 to 550 g in 2024 and 700 g in 2025, then shifted to 450 g in the available 2026 records. This recent contrast is consistent with the reported difficulty finding larger pollock during the 2026 B season. Changes in these distributions can reflect growth, recruitment, the areas fished and the mixture of vessels represented in the observations.</p>
<p>Weekly displays show how size patterns develop within the A-season and B-season windows (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-seasonal-weekly-weight-a">Figure 9</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-seasonal-weekly-weight-b">Figure 10</a>). </p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level2" id="sec-bycatch"><h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-bycatch">3.2 Bycatch</h2>
<p>Pacific ocean perch (3,995 t) and Pacific cod (3,315 t) were the largest bycatch categories in the pollock fishery in 2025, followed by flathead sole (1,813 t). Preliminary 2026 estimates through October 24 were 2,412 t of Pacific ocean perch, 6,549 t of Pacific cod, and 3,367 t of flathead sole. See <a href="#tbl-fmp-species-in-pollock">Table 6</a>.</p><p>Pollock catch in identified non-pollock fisheries declined from 46,996 t in 2024 to 29,263 t in 2025. Rock sole, yellowfin sole, and Pacific cod fisheries accounted for 10,776 t, 8,710 t, and 6,427 t, respectively, in 2025. The preliminary 2026 total through October 31 was 34,729 t; the different cutoffs and partial-year coverage qualify comparisons with the other bycatch tables. See <a href="#tbl-pollock-in-other-fisheries">Table 7</a>.</p><p>Prohibited-species bycatch is summarized in <a href="#tbl-prohibited-species-catch">Table 8</a>. Chinook catches increased from 8,054 fish in 2024 to 19,825 in 2025, and non-Chinook catches increased from 35,152 to 151,457 fish. Halibut mortality rose from 53 to 66 t. Preliminary 2026 catches through October 24 were 15,153 Chinook, 149,468 non-Chinook, and 56 t of halibut mortality.</p><p>Jellyfish dominated the selected nontarget-species catch by weight. Estimated jellyfish catch declined from 4,402 t in 2024 to 1,769 t in 2025. Miscellaneous fish contributed 99 t in 2025, with smaller catches in each of the other displayed groups. Preliminary jellyfish catch through October 24, 2026 was 4,418 t. These catch estimates describe fishery encounters and should be interpreted with fishing effort, distribution, and reporting coverage. See <a href="#tbl-nontarget-species-bycatch">Table 9</a>.</p></section></section>

<p><span id="data-availability-and-update-requirements"></span></p>
<section class="level2" data-number="4.1" id="fishery-catch-and-age-compositions">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="fishery-catch-and-age-compositions" data-number="4.1"><span class="header-section-number">4.1</span> Fishery data</h2>
<section class="level3" data-number="4.1.1" id="sec-fishery-catch"><h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-fishery-catch" data-number="4.1.1"><span class="header-section-number">4.1.1</span> Catch</h3><p>Annual catch rose from about 0.175 million t in 1964 to the series maximum of 1.875 million t in 1972 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-catch-history">Figure 11</a>). Catch subsequently fluctuated, fell to 0.811 and 0.810 million t in 2009 and 2010, respectively, and recovered to 1.326 million t in 2025. The 2026 records total 1.268 million t through October 17 and represent a partial year. Records before 1991 provide annual totals; later records distinguish the A-season and northwest and southeast B-season catches.</p><p>The annual assessment catch includes retained and discarded commercial pollock across gears and targets in the Bering Sea, with CDQ counted once and the separately reported Bogoslof and Aleutian Islands catches excluded. The catch update uses the catch estimates for 1991–2026, with pre-1991 model inputs retained. The revised totals are 1,311,260.74 t in 2024, 1,326,215.61 t in 2025 and 1,312,504.58 t in 2026. The 2026 estimate is the annual input selected for this assessment. Explicit Bogoslof (518) and outside-stock area codes are excluded. The 1998 records with blank area codes remain included under their Bering Sea classification. Noncommercial removals remain separately documented in <a href="#sec-other-removals">Appendix C</a>.</p></section><section class="level3" data-number="4.1.2" id="sec-fishery-age-compositions"><h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-fishery-age-compositions" data-number="4.1.2"><span class="header-section-number">4.1.2</span> Age compositions</h3><p>Fishery catch-at-age estimates for 1964–2025 are summarized in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-fishery-catch-at-age">Table 5</a>. Ages 15 and older are pooled as 15+. Where complete annual catch numbers are unavailable, we calculate numbers at age from the assessment proportions, annual fishery weight-at-age and catch biomass.</p><p>We estimate fishery age compositions from biological samples collected by at-sea observers and during shore-side offloading. The sampling records include fish measured for length frequencies, paired weight–length measurements, and age estimates (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-fishery-length-samples">Table 10</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-fishery-weight-length-samples">Table 11</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-fishery-age-samples">Table 12</a>). The processing keeps recent unsexed fish separate rather than assigning them to males or females. Within each sex and sampling stratum, we expand length frequencies to the associated catch biomass using mean weight at length. Age–length keys allocate the expanded numbers to ages; we then sum the numbers across strata and sexes and normalize them to give annual proportions <span class="citation" data-cites="kimura1989 barbeaux2005 ianelli2024safe">(<a href="#ref-kimura1989" role="doc-biblioref">Kimura 1989</a>; <a href="#ref-barbeaux2005" role="doc-biblioref">Barbeaux et al. 2005</a>; <a href="#ref-ianelli2024safe" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2024</a>)</span>. Earlier assessments provide the pre-1991 age compositions. For the 2024–2025 update, the processing strata are January–May across Bering Sea areas, followed by June–December split into northwest (NMFS reporting areas 520 and above) and southeast (areas below 520). The 2024 assessment describes January–June and July–December groups; the current sampling groups use the calendar periods defined above. The new length and age records cover all 12 months. </p><p>The linked bootstrap represents variation among sampling units and among length and age observations within those units. Its composition precision estimates inform the selected likelihood sample sizes: 443, 578 and 530 for 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. They represent effective information for fitting the annual proportions, rather than numbers of fish measured or aged (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-weights">Section 4.3.1</a>). The model fits annual sex-combined proportions at ages 1–14 and 15+. Fishery age observations end in 2025.</p><p>The 2024–2025 age-estimate data are from pelagic trawl fisheries. For 2025, FT-NIRS predictions from model a00-d3 are expressed on an independent traditional microscopic-ageing (TMA) basis using 668 paired estimates (<a href="#sec-ftnir-appendix">Appendix G</a>). Within each FT-NIRS age, the paired observations define the proportions assigned to each tester age. These probabilities redistribute the catch-expanded numbers among ages while preserving their total. Source age 13 lacks paired tester observations; its conditional probabilities are the midpoint of the age-12 and age-14 rows. The 2025 source and tester ages range from 2 to 15, and the assessment fits ages 1–14 and 15+. The likelihood uses the selected input sample size of 530. Uncertainty in the conversion key and the age-13 interpolation is additional to the sampling uncertainty represented by that input weight.</p><p>The 2024 fishery age composition is expressed on the independent TMA basis using 693 paired reader–tester observations. For source age 13, the key pools TMA-minus-FT-NIRS age offsets from the same year’s source ages 9–12 (34 pairs) and adds those offsets to age 13. Empirical key rows retain their observed probabilities. </p></section><section class="level3" data-number="4.1.3" id="sec-fishery-weights">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-fishery-weights" data-number="4.1.3"><span class="header-section-number">4.1.3</span> Weight-at-age</h3>
<p>Mean weight-at-age connects the assessment’s estimates of fish numbers to catch biomass and harvest projections. Seasonal and spatial differences in fish condition and fishery distribution affect these means. Fishery sampling is therefore organized by season and area, with stratum estimates combined using the corresponding catch information. Completed-year observations provide the basis for estimating weights for the observation year and forecasting the weights needed for future catches.</p>
<p>For recent fishery samples, Fourier-transform near-infrared spectroscopy (FT-NIR) of otoliths provides predicted ages. Year-specific paired FT-NIR and traditional morphological ageing (TMA) observations align these predictions with the TMA age basis. Estimated abundance and biomass in each FT-NIR age bin are redistributed using the same conditional tester-age key. Mean weight at a target age is then converted biomass divided by converted abundance. For the 15+ group, biomass and abundance are pooled before taking their ratio. The conversion retains each source bin’s mean weight when allocating it among tester ages. Its reported uncertainty conditions on the selected key; the supported ages and approved tail-allocation rules are documented in <a href="#sec-ftnir-appendix">Appendix G</a>.</p>
<p>The weight-model approach described in Section 14.5 of the 2024 assessment <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2024safe">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2024safe" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2024</a>)</span> links growth within cohorts to annual changes in condition. A smooth mean age pattern defines the typical weight increments. A cohort’s weight in the previous year provides the starting point for the next age, while annual random effects allow variation in starting weight and growth. Observed mean weights and their variances inform this model, separating sampling precision from variability among years. The fitted model supplies predictions for missing observations and forecasts for future years. Model 26.0 uses the resulting weight schedules as fixed biological inputs.</p>
<p>The annual fishery weights in <a href="#tbl-fishery-weights-projections">Table 28</a> retain the historical observational inputs through 2025, with fitted values for missing 2025 ages 13 and 14. The 2026 predictions and 2027–2028 forecasts use the standalone WtAgeRE fit. Ages 1–2 retain the 2024 inputs, the 1964–1990 schedule remains fixed, and the terminal age is 15+.</p>
<p>Cohort growth and annual changes in condition link observed weights to the schedules used for catch and spawning projections. Observed fishery and BTS weights and the selected fishery-scale estimates for 2014–2028 are shown in <a href="#fig-waa-omit-bts2026">Figure 23</a>. The forecast follows the 2026 age-3 cohort from 0.368 kg to 0.482 kg at age 4 in 2027 and 0.601 kg at age 5 in 2028. The 2026 biological weight schedules are compared with the selected 2027 catch and spawning projection weights in <a href="#fig-model262-current-biological-schedules">Figure 35</a>.</p>
</section></section>
<section class="level2" data-number="4.2" id="survey-data">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="survey-data" data-number="4.2"><span class="header-section-number">4.2</span> Survey data</h2>
<section class="level3" data-number="4.2.1" id="bottom-trawl-survey">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="bottom-trawl-survey" data-number="4.2.1"><span class="header-section-number">4.2.1</span> Bottom-trawl survey</h3>
<p>The AFSC bottom-trawl survey provides indices of pollock abundance and population age structure, complementing the acoustic-trawl survey’s sampling of the midwater component. Historical and recent sampling effort is summarized in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-bts-sampling-effort">Table 13</a>. Annual surveys began in 1979, with standardized gear and methods from 1982 <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2024safe">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2024safe" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2024</a>)</span>. The 2025 and 2026 observations extend the 42 survey years available for the 2024 assessment to 44 observed years during 1982–2026. The survey was absent in 2020; that year remains a gap in the observation series. The biomass estimates and assessment CVs are listed in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-bts-biomass">Table 14</a>. Availability to bottom-trawl gear varies with age and vertical distribution. Ages 2–3 are often relatively scarce in the catches because juveniles tend to occupy the water column <span class="citation" data-cites="monnahan2021 oleary2022">(<a href="#ref-monnahan2021" role="doc-biblioref">Monnahan et al. 2021</a>; <a href="#ref-oleary2022" role="doc-biblioref">O’Leary et al. 2022</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Bottom temperature appears to influence the distribution of pollock available to the bottom-trawl survey. The AKsf survey-mapping example <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2026aksf">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2026aksf" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli 2026</a>)</span> places annual CPUE distributions alongside the 0, 2 and 4 °C bottom-temperature contours for 2018, 2019 and 2021–2026 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-bts-cpue-temperature-aksf">Figure 12</a>). High CPUE is concentrated along parts of the western and southern shelf, with several dense patches near the 2 °C contour in 2022, 2024 and 2026. The more extensive warm-water conditions in 2018–2019 contrast with the broader areas of cold bottom water in later panels, while the locations and extent of the pollock concentrations also change.</p>
<p>These patterns suggest that temperature helps structure near-bottom habitat and survey availability, with concentrations often near the margins of colder shelf water. Depth, prey, age composition and vertical movements can also contribute to the pattern. The maps show spatial associations between survey distributions and temperature. Other environmental and biological factors may also contribute. They use locally interpolated, density-dependent-corrected CPUE within survey coverage. The example’s correction version and adoption status are unspecified, so its CPUE surface serves as a descriptive illustration alongside the assessment indices.</p>
<p>The standard EBS survey expanded northwest in 1987. Sampling in the separate NBS region has varied among years, while pollock distribution has shifted between regions. Model-based estimates integrate station observations, including zero catches, across the EBS and NBS and account for spatial and temporal variation <span class="citation" data-cites="OLeary2020">(<a href="#ref-OLeary2020" role="doc-biblioref">O’Leary et al. 2020</a>)</span>. The biomass index uses sdmTMB and abundance at age uses tinyVAST, replacing the earlier VAST implementation. The complete selected abundance-at-age series incorporates historical revisions as well as the recent observations (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-bts-abundance-at-age">Table 15</a>). The regional coverage, model specifications, annual covariance and remaining production-source qualifications are described in <a href="#sec-bts-spatiotemporal-appendix">Appendix H</a>. Estimates for unsampled years are model predictions.</p>
<p>The BTS length distributions show pronounced changes in the sizes represented in the survey (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-bts-length-composition-history">Figure 13</a>). Peaks among small fish and their progression toward larger lengths illustrate cohort growth, while the relative contribution of small and large fish varies among years. These distributions complement the age compositions by showing changes in size directly.</p>
<p>The BTS age compositions show changes in the ages represented in the survey and the progression of cohorts through time (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-bts-age-composition-history">Figure 14</a>). Highlighted bars follow the 1992, 2012 and 2018 year classes through successive ages. The 2012 year class progresses from age 1 in 2013 to age 10 in 2022, while the 2018 year class progresses from age 1 in 2019 to age 8 in 2026. The blank 2020 row marks the gap when the survey was absent.</p>
<p>The age compositions combined traditional age readings and FT-NIRS estimates. We converted the 2026 FT-NIRS estimates to traditional ages using 307 screened paired readings (<a href="#sec-ftnir-appendix">Appendix G</a>). The conversion preserved total survey abundance and pooled ages 15 and older into the 15+ group.</p>
<p>Spatiotemporal estimation of BTS weight-at-age, adopted in 2022, replaces the earlier conversion of mean length to weight <span class="citation" data-cites="indivero2023">(<a href="#ref-indivero2023" role="doc-biblioref">Indivero et al. 2023</a>)</span>. The full BTS-derived weight schedules used for population biomass are presented in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-bts-historical-weights">Table 16</a>; the compact biological-input summary retains the recent fishery and spawning schedules and fixed biological parameters. We applied the screened 2026 age key consistently to BTS weight-at-age means and their delta-method standard errors, retaining the joint covariance treatment. We used the same key for the provisional ATS abundance and biomass-derived weights, including the weights used to predict the 2026 AVO index. We refitted the standalone random-effects weight-at-age model with the revised BTS means and standard errors under the existing equations, likelihood and source-covariance treatment, preserving fishery observations and the 2025 conversion key. These uncertainty calculations exclude empirical age-key uncertainty. The conversion, weight calculations and assessment use are described in <a href="#sec-ftnir-treatment">Appendix G</a>.</p>
<p>The missing 2020 survey and subsequent 2021 observation affect interpretation of the time series. Retrospective comparisons describe changes in population estimates as observations accumulate (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-paired-current-retrospectives">Section 6.1.5</a>).</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="4.2.2" id="sec-ats">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-ats" data-number="4.2.2"><span class="header-section-number">4.2.2</span> Acoustic-trawl survey</h3>
<p>The 2026 ATS ages are provisional: we apply the BTS age–length key (ALK) to ATS population length-frequency estimates. FT-NIRS ages from the 2026 ATS samples will be available in 2027.</p>
<p>Acoustic-trawl surveys (ATS) are typically conducted every other year and estimate the off-bottom component of the pollock stock, complementing the annual BTS index of near-bottom pollock. Historical and acoustic-trawl sampling effort is summarized in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-sampling-effort">Table 17</a>. The 2026 collections retain their regional scope, while unavailable direct age counts remain NA.</p>
<!-- Generated from the shared wiki source by scripts/sync_survey_sections.py. -->
<p>Estimated pollock biomass for the EBS shelf has averaged about 3.202 million t since 1994, when the revised time series begins (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-biomass">Table 18</a>). The revised estimates include the water column down to 0.5 m above the seafloor; the historical midwater index extended to 3 m above the seafloor. Low recruitment during the relatively warm early 2000s was subsequently reflected in lower survey biomass during the cold period of 2006–2012 <span class="citation" data-cites="honkalehto2015">(<a href="#ref-honkalehto2015" role="doc-biblioref">Honkalehto and McCarthy 2015</a>)</span>. With growth of the strong 2012 year class, biomass exceeded 4 million t in 2014 and 2016, another warm period. The 2026 regional estimates included the Steller sea lion conservation area (SCA) and the Northern Extension (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-regions">Table 19</a>). The SCA is a traditionally reported subset of the survey used to evaluate pollock abundance in areas considered sensitive to Steller sea lions.</p>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="sec-ats-age-history">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-ats-age-history">Historical abundance at age</h4>
<p>The historical series showed strong pulses of age-1 fish in 1997, 2007, 2009, 2014 and 2024 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-age-history">Table 20</a>). The provisional 2026 estimates were largest at ages 2 and 3: 3.73 and 3.96 billion fish, respectively, compared with 2.03 billion age-1 fish.</p>
<p>The ATS age compositions show pulses of young fish and the progression of cohorts through successive surveys (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-ats-age-composition-history">Figure 15</a>). The highlighted 2018 year class appears at age 4 in 2022, age 6 in 2024 and age 8 in 2026. Ages 2 and 3 dominate the provisional 2026 composition. The 2026 estimates use the BTS age–length key applied to ATS population length frequencies; FT-NIRS ages from the 2026 ATS samples are expected in 2027. Blank years represent gaps in the age-composition series.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="survey-design-and-results">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="survey-design-and-results">2026 survey design and results</h4>
<p>The 2026 ATS covered the EBS shelf from approximately 60 m depth to the shelf break between 30 May and 4 August. Core-area transects were spaced at 20 nmi; selected transects extended into the Northern Extension at 40 nmi spacing. Survey timing was similar to 2022, with a longer duration in 2026 because of special projects. The area east of 170° W was surveyed from 30 May to 25 June, and the area west of 170° W from 26 June to 4 August.</p>
<p>The 2026 core-area estimate was 12.7 billion fish and 3.682 million t of biomass (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-core-estimates">Table 21</a>). Biomass increased by 28% relative to the 2024 estimate of 2.875 million t (11.4 billion fish). The 2026 biomass estimate was 4% below the 2022 estimate of 3.834 million t (9.67 billion fish) and 16% above the 1994–2024 survey mean of 3.176 million t. These are survey estimates; assessment intake and adoption remain separate decisions.</p>
<p>Provisional 2026 ATS age compositions over supported lengths were estimated by applying the FT-NIRS-based BTS age–length key to ATS abundance-at-length (<a href="#sec-ftnir-appendix">Appendix G</a>). Midwater pollock were concentrated between the 100 m contour and the shelf break, particularly northwest of Unimak Pass and between Zhemchug and Pervenets canyons. Length distributions suggested that presumed age-1 fish (&lt;20 cm fork length) formed dense schools on the northwestern shelf, with smaller concentrations east of the Pribilof Islands and near Unimak Pass. Presumed age-3+ fish accounted for most biomass, with 74% of their biomass west of 170° W.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="sec-ats-derived-ages">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-ats-derived-ages">Provisional abundance at age from the 2026 BTS keys</h4>
<p>We estimated provisional ages by matching ATS lengths to the 2026 BTS FT-NIRS age–length key, then converting those ages to traditional ages using paired readings. Ages 2 and 3 dominated the resulting distribution (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-derived-abundance">Table 22</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-ats-derived-ages">Figure 16</a>). Fish beyond the key’s length range represented less than 0.001% of core-area abundance. The technical appendix describes the keys, calibration and allocation assumptions.</p>
<p><span id="data-records"></span></p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="sec-ats-derived-weights">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-ats-derived-weights">Biomass and mean weight-at-age</h4>
<p>We applied the same age keys to biomass and divided biomass by abundance to estimate mean weights at age. The resulting mean weights are presented in <a href="#tbl-ats-tma-weights">Table 23</a> and <a href="#fig-ats-derived-weights">Figure 17</a>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="survey-uncertainty-and-assessment-treatment">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="survey-uncertainty-and-assessment-treatment">Survey uncertainty and assessment treatment</h4>
<p>We estimated ATS biomass sampling error with the established one-dimensional geostatistical method, which accounted for spatial patterns along survey transects <span class="citation" data-cites="petitgas1993 walline2007 williamson1996">(<a href="#ref-petitgas1993" role="doc-biblioref">Petitgas 1993</a>; <a href="#ref-walline2007" role="doc-biblioref">Walline 2007</a>; <a href="#ref-williamson1996" role="doc-biblioref">Williamson and Traynor 1996</a>)</span>. The 2026 sampling error was 3.4% of estimated biomass, compared with a historical average of 4.4%. Complete core-area coverage at 20 nmi transect spacing likely contributed to the lower error.</p>
<p>For assessment use, we increased the survey errors to allow for additional uncertainty, including target strength and trawl selectivity. We scaled the assessment coefficients of variation to average 20% over 1994–2026 and assigned a value of 45% to 2000 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-biomass">Table 18</a>).</p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="spatial-and-historical-patterns">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="spatial-and-historical-patterns">Spatial and historical patterns</h4>
<p>The ATS index used in the assessment covered the water column down to 0.5 m above the seafloor, while the historical heatmap showed biomass from near the surface to 3 m above the bottom (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-ats-historical-heatmap">Figure 18</a>). Biomass was low during 2008–2012, especially in 2008–2009, and increased in 2014–2016. The maps also showed shifts in the strength and location of concentrations along the western and southern shelf. The Northern Extension contained an additional 0.078 million t beyond the 3.682 million t core-area estimate (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-regions">Table 19</a>).</p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="biomass-time-series-and-observation-errors">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="biomass-time-series-and-observation-errors">Biomass time series and observation errors</h4>
<p>The series contained 20 survey estimates between 1994 and 2026. We plotted approximate 95% sampling intervals around each biomass estimate using the survey standard errors (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-ats-biomass">Figure 19</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-ats-biomass">Table 18</a>). Gaps in the annual series marked years without a survey estimate. These intervals described survey sampling variability; the assessment used larger errors to allow for additional uncertainty.</p>
<p><span id="2026-transect-distribution"></span></p>
<p>Biomass varied strongly along the survey tracks. Concentrations were highest on parts of the western and southern shelf and generally lower in the far north (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-ats-transects">Figure 20</a>). The map included the Northern Extension and showed GMT contours of mean biomass per sampling interval (tons per EDSU). The map uses approximately 10-nautical-mile cell means, with the smoothed surface displayed within 30 km of sampled cell centers.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="4.2.3" id="sec-avo">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-avo" data-number="4.2.3"><span class="header-section-number">4.2.3</span> Acoustic vessel-of-opportunity index</h3>
<!-- Generated from the shared wiki source by scripts/sync_survey_sections.py. -->
<p>The acoustic vessel-of-opportunity (AVO) index provides a relative-abundance observation for age-1 and older midwater pollock within the U.S. EEZ <span class="citation" data-cites="honkalehto2011 lauffenburger2025avo">(<a href="#ref-honkalehto2011" role="doc-biblioref">Honkalehto et al. 2011</a>; <a href="#ref-lauffenburger2025avo" role="doc-biblioref">Lauffenburger et al. 2025</a>)</span>. The 2026 observations were collected at 38 kHz from 29 May to 5 August aboard the summer bottom-trawl charter vessels. The index covers the water column from 3 m above the seabed to 16 m below the surface.</p>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="assessment-index">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="assessment-index">Annual index</h4>
<p>Relative AVO backscatter is lowest at 0.299 in 2009 and highest at 1.55 in 2015 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-avo-index">Table 25</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-avo-index">Figure 21</a>). It is 0.863 in 2024, 1.07 in 2025 and 1.12 in 2026, with sampling CVs of 2.72%, 5.26% and 4.55%, respectively. The 2025 and 2026 sampling confidence intervals overlap. The display series covers 2009–2026, excluding 2020, when no bottom-trawl survey took place. Each annual area-integrated estimate is divided by the mean of the 17 estimates to give a mean-one series. The table also retains total pollock backscatter, in millions of square metres, with sampling errors and scaled confidence intervals. This is an acoustic backscattering cross section, rather than geographic area <span class="citation" data-cites="lauffenburger2025avo">(<a href="#ref-lauffenburger2025avo" role="doc-biblioref">Lauffenburger et al. 2025</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>For the nine paired survey years in the 2009–2026 display period, AVO total pollock backscatter and revised ATS biomass have a squared Pearson correlation of 0.89. This association is descriptive: AVO covers 3 m above the seabed to 16 m below the surface, while the revised ATS index extends from 0.5 m above the seabed to 16 m below the surface. The vertical domains differ. The 2026 AVO report gives 0.90 using an ATS 2026 estimate of 3.62 million t; the comparison here uses the revised ATS estimate of 3.682 million t <span class="citation" data-cites="afscmace2026avo">(<a href="#ref-afscmace2026avo" role="doc-biblioref">AFSC-RACE MACE 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="spatial-distribution-and-sampling-coverage">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="spatial-distribution-and-sampling-coverage">Spatial distribution and sampling coverage</h4>
<p>Strong backscatter occurs along western EBS tracks in the recent maps, with weaker returns interspersed along central and southeastern tracks (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-avo-all-years">Figure 22</a>). The annual panels use a common map extent and color scale while showing differences in track coverage.</p>
<p>The longer series also contains alternating strong and weak returns along the sampled shelf (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-avo-all-years">Figure 22</a>). The year 2020 is omitted because AVO observations are unavailable. Survey coverage and processing vary among years. Inferences about population redistribution require comparable sampling and integration across years.</p>
<p>The number of observed survey intervals ranges from 5,557 in 2009 to 12,229 in 2024 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-avo-coverage">Table 26</a>). Zero shares fall from 56.3% in 2009 to 7.8% in 2015, vary subsequently, and are 14.9%, 5.0% and 14.2% in 2024–2026, respectively.</p>
<p>The maps summarize observed pollock backscatter in approximately 20-nautical-mile cells, including zeros. GMT gridding and contours show the mean backscatter in m² nmi⁻² on a common color scale. Surfaces extend up to 45 km from sampled cell centers; more distant areas remain masked. The annual AVO index integrates backscatter over the survey area and is reported in million m². Survey coverage and processing vary among years, so comparisons of spatial patterns depend on comparable sampling.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="sec-avo-assessment-cvs">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-avo-assessment-cvs">Assessment use and observation uncertainty</h4>
<p>The AVO assessment index is 2.01 million m² in 2024, 2.50 million m² in 2025 and 2.60 million m² in 2026 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-avo-assessment-series">Table 27</a>). Its 20 observations cover 2006–2026, excluding 2020. The assessment uses the newly processed 2011 and 2013 estimates and their sampling errors <span class="citation" data-cites="afscmace2026avo">(<a href="#ref-afscmace2026avo" role="doc-biblioref">AFSC-RACE MACE 2026</a>)</span>. The 2006–2008 estimates retain the legacy rescaling described in the 2024 assessment <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2024safe">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2024safe" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2024</a>)</span>. </p>
<p>Survey sampling errors describe one-dimensional geostatistical variability. The assessment applies additional observation-error inflation to an arithmetic mean CV of 23% across its 20 observations. The two newly processed years use the existing modern-year error inflation rule, followed by common recalibration of all 20 CVs to that mean. Assessment errors differ from sampling errors and from the ATS mean assessment CV of 20%.</p>
<p>For the Normal index likelihood, arithmetic observation SEs equal the retained assessment index multiplied by its selected CV. For the display series, let <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_t</annotation></semantics></math> denote the original index, <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mover><mi>I</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar I</annotation></semantics></math> its 17-year mean and <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>/</mi><mover><mi>I</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_t=I_t/\bar I</annotation></semantics></math>. The same constant rescales its index, SEs and confidence limits, leaving the CV unchanged:</p>
<p><math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi></mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo form="postfix" stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>±</mo><mn>1.96</mn><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mover><mi>I</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover></mfrac><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathrm{SE}(R_t)=R_t\,\mathrm{CV}_t,\qquad
[L_t,U_t]=\frac{I_t\pm1.96\,I_t\mathrm{CV}_t}{\bar I}.
</annotation></semantics></math></p>
<p>The source 95% interval is represented by the half-width <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.96</mn><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.96 I_t\mathrm{CV}_t</annotation></semantics></math>, checked for every observed year. The displayed intervals describe survey sampling uncertainty with normalization treated as a change of units; assessment error inflation is a separate model input.</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="4.3" id="sec-other-data">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-other-data" data-number="4.3"><span class="header-section-number">4.3</span> Other data</h2>
<p>Model 26.0 fitted the 12 historical CPUE observations from 1965–1976 using fishery selectivity and fishery weights at age. We retained the observations and errors from the reference fit through 2024.</p>
<p><strong><em>Fixed biological assumptions</em></strong></p>
<p>We retained the 2024 biological assumptions <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2024safe">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2024safe" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2024</a>)</span>. Natural mortality was 0.9 yr⁻¹ at age 1, 0.45 yr⁻¹ at age 2 and 0.3 yr⁻¹ at ages 3–15+. Maturity at ages 1–15+ was 0, .008, .289, .641, .842, .901, .947, .963, .970, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. The model calculated April spawning biomass one quarter-year after the start of the year and applied a female fraction of 0.5 once to sex-combined abundance. We used a 15-by-15 identity matrix for ageing error, matching the archived ADMB configuration. This likelihood assumption treated ages as exact after data preparation, which used FT-NIRS age conversion and age–length keys.</p>
<p>All weight schedules covered ages 1–15+ for the combined sexes in kg per fish. The model used fishery weights to calculate catch biomass, BTS weights to calculate population biomass and A-season weights to calculate spawning biomass.</p>
<p><strong><em>Population and spawning weights</em></strong></p>
<p>Population weights use BTS observations through 2026. Three historical values retain their previous treatment; details are in the technical supplement. For spawning biomass, we replaced the older weights at ages 3–15+ with A-season fitted values for 2024–2025 and projections for 2026. Within the common-year comparison, this update changed the 13 values at ages 3–15+ in 2024. We retained baseline weights at ages 1–2; age-2 maturity was .008.</p>
<p><strong><em>ATS and AVO weights</em></strong></p>
<p>We retained each historical schedule through 2024 and carried its weights forward to 2025. After BTS-ALK and conditional TMA preparation, we calculated provisional 2026 ATS weights by dividing biomass by the corresponding abundance. For age 15+, we pooled biomass and abundance before division. <a href="#sec-ftnir-appendix">Appendix G</a> documented the supported lengths and unallocated tail. We used the 2026 ATS vector as a proxy for AVO weights, although the historical schedules differed.</p>
<p><a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-fishery-weights">Section 4.1.3</a> described the rationale for changing weight estimation. Weight-schedule uncertainty remained separate from the assessment’s conditional parameter uncertainty. Native forecasts repeated the 2026 weight vectors. </p>
<section class="level3" data-number="4.3.1" id="sec-weights">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-weights" data-number="4.3.1"><span class="header-section-number">4.3.1</span> Age-composition input sample sizes</h3>
<p>The full-data Model 23.0 fit uses fishery composition N=443, 578 and 530 for 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model23-age-sample-sizes">Table 24</a>). These are the rounded continuity-scaled harmonic estimates from the corrected sampler bootstrap, applied in the completed full-data Model 23.0 fit at the author’s direction. The bootstrap preserves linked sampling units within fishery strata and uses 10,000 replicates per year. ATS 2026 uses N=94, and BTS retains the selected 2026 N, shown as 131. Fishery N is fixed at 10 in each year from 1964–1977. The three composition-likelihood multipliers are 1.</p>
<p>Model 26.0 fits age compositions with a multinomial model. The baseline retains likelihood sample sizes from the bridge workbook. These likelihood sample sizes differ from counts of fish sampled and from diagnostic effective sample sizes. For every fishery or survey year, the final assessment must provide the raw sampling information, starting sample size, adjustment method, and final sample size used in the likelihood. The 2020 biomass estimate remains a separate fitted survey observation.</p>
<p>One-step-ahead (OSA) residuals compare an observation with its conditional prediction after preceding age categories have been considered. The OSA and Francis comparisons document the selected weights and observed-data residual patterns in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-francis-comparison">Section 6.1.6</a>.</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="5" id="sec-approach">
<h1 data-number="5"><span class="header-section-number">5</span> Analytic approach</h1>
<section class="level2" data-number="5.1" id="main-and-comparison-models">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="main-and-comparison-models" data-number="5.1"><span class="header-section-number">5.1</span> Main and comparison models</h2>
<p>Model 26.0 (Rceattle) is the adopted model for Tier 3 calculations and specifications. Models 23.0 and 23.2 provide comparisons with the previous assessment and the transition in model structure. Other sensitivities separate the early Foreign fishery (1964–1990) from the later domestic fishery (1991–2026) and vary the penalty on declining selectivity. Model 26.1.2 is the Early-late fishery split sensitivity. The fits and retrospective comparisons hold the process standard deviations fixed at the values estimated by its marginal model. Model 26.0 uncertainty and retrospective diagnostics are described below.</p>
<section class="level3" data-number="5.1.1" id="sec-model23-data-impacts">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model23-data-impacts" data-number="5.1.1"><span class="header-section-number">5.1.1</span> Model 23.0 and impact of new data</h3>
<p>As in past years, we incrementally introduced new data relative to the previous assessment while retaining the Model 23.0 formulation. We began with total catch through 2026, incorporating the revised catch estimates for 1991–2026 (2026: 1,312,504.58 t) and extending the model endpoint and parameter and projection horizons to accommodate the added years. At this first step, fishery age compositions and survey observations retained their historical coverage. We then updated weight-at-age and A-season spawning weights, followed by fishery catch-at-age data and their information weights.</p>
<p>The survey updates followed in sequence: the bottom-trawl survey (BTS), the acoustic-trawl survey (ATS), and the acoustic vessels of opportunity (AVO) index. BTS retained the 2020 survey gap and annual information weights, including the real-valued 2026 input. ATS incorporated the selected age-1 rule and provisional 2026 age information, and AVO incorporated its annual observations and assessment-error recalibration. Historical revisions and uncertainty recalibration were included with each survey’s update (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-ats">Section 4.2.2</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-avo">Section 4.2.3</a>).</p>
<p>Each step includes all preceding updates, so its estimated effect depends on the order in which the data were added. The resulting 2026 estimates are summarized in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model23-data-impacts">Table 29</a>, and the cumulative annual point estimates are shown in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model23-data-impacts">Figure 24</a>. These comparisons use matched definitions of population-weight biomass, female spawning biomass, age-1 recruitment and maximum realized fishing mortality across ages. Model equations are given in <a href="#sec-model-equations">the model-equations appendix</a>.</p>
<p>The saved 2027 spawning-biomass and young-abundance projections from the cumulative input-update analyses are compared in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model23-2027-increments">Figure 25</a>. These diagnostic projections retain the earlier 2026 catch estimate of 1,310,000 t; the 2026 estimates above use the revised catch inputs. The display starts with Catch + 2026 endpoint, followed by + Fishery age data and the subsequent survey updates. The intervening weight-at-age and A-season spawning-weight updates remain incorporated in the fishery-age and later fits. Abundance at ages 1–3 is measured at the start of 2027, before removals; spawning biomass includes mortality to spawning time. Projection settings are detailed in the technical supplement. Management projections retain their separate catch, selectivity, weight and recruitment assumptions (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-projections">Section 7</a>).</p>
<p>The input sequence and configuration comparison answer different questions. The former retains the Model 23.0 formulation while adding observations and updating schedules. The latter compares formulations on matched observations and biology (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-updated-configuration-effects">Table 30</a>). </p>
<p>Approximate distributions compare the change in spawning biomass from 2026 to 2027 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model23-ssb-change-density">Figure 26</a>) and the historical change in total abundance at ages 1–4 from 2025 to 2026 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model23-young-n-change-density">Figure 27</a>). They show the same selected cumulative sequence, followed by Models 23.2 and 26.0. Their input and projection settings are documented in the technical supplement. Each distribution retains its matching fitted-parameter covariance between years and, for abundance, among ages. The normal approximations are conditional on the model and biological and projection assumptions. </p>
<p>Among the additions in the saved 2027 projection comparison, ATS produced the largest increase in female spawning biomass: from 2.685 to 2.975 million t, an increase of about 290,000 t (10.8%) relative to the preceding BTS step. AVO increased projected spawning biomass a further 61,000 t (2.0%), to 3.036 million t. The effects on estimated 2026 spawning biomass differed: fishery age data produced the largest increase, about 213,000 t (8.4%); ATS reduced it by about 73,000 t (2.6%), and AVO increased it by about 47,000 t (1.7%). These are successive changes within the specified sequence, with each survey contrast including its historical revisions and error calibration.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="5.1.2" id="sec-model232-updated">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model232-updated" data-number="5.1.2"><span class="header-section-number">5.1.2</span> Model 23.2 fitted to the 2026 assessment data</h3>
<p>Model 23.2 is a structural bridge between the ADMB continuity model and the Rceattle configuration. Its annual spawning-biomass and recruitment trajectories retain their documented scope. The established zero-variance management quantities are excluded from management comparisons. Current configuration effects use verified saved population outputs and their stated units. The comparison of Models 23.0 and 23.2 includes matching local asymptotic uncertainty ranges (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model230-vs232">Figure 28</a>). </p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="5.1.3" id="sec-model262-updated">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model262-updated" data-number="5.1.3"><span class="header-section-number">5.1.3</span> Model 26.0 fitted to the 2026 assessment data</h3>
<p>Model 26.0 uses one fishery and fixed weight-at-age schedules. The updated base model fit retains its native working-likelihood, parameter bounds, selectivity forms, priors and fixed biological assumptions. We check outputs against the written inputs and saved native quantities. Population-weight biomass, female spawning biomass, age-1 recruitment and maximum fishing mortality retain distinct definitions. Their annual estimates and matching local asymptotic uncertainty are compared with Model 23.2 in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model232-vs262">Figure 29</a>. </p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="5.1.4" id="sec-model261-configuration">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model261-configuration" data-number="5.1.4"><span class="header-section-number">5.1.4</span> Model 26.1: Foreign and Modern domestic fisheries</h3>
<p>The split-fishery alternatives distinguish Foreign fishing in 1964–1990 from Modern domestic fishing in 1991–2026. Model 26.1.0 supplies the fitted split-fishery comparison; Model 26.1.1 reduces the declining-selectivity penalty, and the zero-penalty case removes it.  Model 26.1.2 extends that formulation by estimating the Modern annual selectivity-process SD while integrating over annual selectivity effects. The Foreign process SD remains fixed. Local uncertainty uses the verified marginal information for this alternative; its observation diagnostics condition on the fitted annual effects.</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="6" id="sec-results">
<h1 data-number="6"><span class="header-section-number">6</span> Results</h1>
<section class="level2" data-number="6.1" id="model-26.0-assessment">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="model-26.0-assessment" data-number="6.1"><span class="header-section-number">6.1</span> Model 26.0 assessment</h2>
<p>Model 26.0 provides the main estimates of stock size and the basis for the Tier 3 catch limits presented here. Results from the other model configurations, including Model 26.1.2, show how alternative assumptions affect the assessment. Additional analyses describe uncertainty in Model 26.0 estimates and how those estimates change when recent years of data are removed. Comparisons with past assessments use the data and catch advice reported in each assessment year.</p>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.1.1" id="sec-model262-current-estimates">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model262-current-estimates" data-number="6.1.1"><span class="header-section-number">6.1.1</span> Population estimates and uncertainty</h3>
<p>The Model 26.0 base model estimates 2026 total biomass at <strong>12.162 million t</strong>, female spawning biomass at <strong>3.057 million t</strong>, age-1 recruitment at <strong>36.3 billion fish</strong>, and maximum fishing mortality across ages at <strong>0.299 per year</strong> (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model262-current-terminal-estimates">Table 31</a>).</p>
<p>The local asymptotic 95% ranges in the tables use the revised fit’s native covariance. The uncertainty figure is shown in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-current-full-uncertainty">Figure 30</a>.  Annual estimates and ranges appear in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model262-current-annual-estimates">Table 32</a>.</p>
<p>Regularized-posterior intervals use all 5,000 existing draws, using the final reported summaries (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model260-regularized-posterior">Table 33</a>). The 2026 female spawning-biomass median is <strong>2.946 million t</strong>, with a central 95% credible interval of <strong>2.450–3.584 million t</strong>. Total-biomass median is <strong>11.462 million t</strong>, with interval <strong>9.215–14.719 million t</strong>. Age-1 recruitment median is <strong>31.1518 billion fish</strong>, with interval <strong>12.2880–91.0616 billion fish</strong>.
