These are the final reported MCMC summaries; production point estimates and asymptotic intervals retain their separate roles.</p>
<p>Numbers-at-age track cohorts through the population (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-current-numbers-uncertainty">Figure 31</a>). This shows periods of how recruitment and changes in fishing mortality by age affect abundance relative to their mean abundance estimates (and uncertainty) propagates through time. Actual point estimates are reported in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model262-current-numbers-at-age">Table 34</a>, while the 2026 abundance-at-age estimates (and asymptotic uncertainties) are shown in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model262-current-terminal-numbers">Table 35</a>.</p>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="comparison-with-the-2024-assessment">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="comparison-with-the-2024-assessment">Comparison with the 2024 assessment</h4>
<p>The 2018 year class remains a large recruitment point estimate (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-recruitment-2024-current">Figure 32</a>). Its age-1 abundance in 2019 is <strong>87.8 billion fish</strong> in the Model 26.0 base model, compared with <strong>81.1 billion</strong> in the accepted 2024 assessment, a revision of <strong>8.3%</strong>. The revision reflects both updated observations and changes in model structure.</p>
<p>The estimate for the same 2024 female spawning biomass changes from <strong>3.389 million t</strong> in the saved 2024 assessment to <strong>3.526 million t</strong> in Model 26.0, a revision of <strong>4.0%</strong>. Within the trajectory, spawning biomass changes from that 2024 estimate to <strong>3.057 million t</strong> in 2026 (<strong>-13.3%</strong>). Total biomass changes from <strong>10.767 million t</strong> to <strong>12.162 million t</strong> over the same years (<strong>13.0%</strong>). These within-trajectory changes differ from shared-year assessment revisions.</p>
<p>The recruitment comparison uses calendar age-1 year and billion-fish units (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-recruitment-2024-current">Figure 32</a>). Model 26.1.2 results are included to examine how recruitment estimates for the early period change relative to the 2024 assessment. Historical values are point estimates. Current error bars use each model’s local asymptotic covariance: the base-model covariance for Model 26.0 and the marginal information for Model 26.1.2. Recent years without a historical estimate are identified. These intervals describe uncertainty around the fitted estimates.</p><p>The two assessments project different spawning-biomass paths through 2028 (<a href="#fig-projection-vintages">Figure 33</a>). The comparison retains each assessment’s Scenario 2 catch assumptions; the current uncertainty band propagates local assessment-parameter uncertainty.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="recruitment-per-unit-of-spawning-biomass">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="recruitment-per-unit-of-spawning-biomass">Recruitment per unit of spawning biomass</h4>
<p>The log recruits-per-spawner diagnostic from the 2024 assessment is updated using the Model 26.0 estimates (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-lnrs">Figure 34</a>). For each year of hatching, age-1 recruitment in the following year is divided by female spawning biomass in the year of hatching. Taking the natural logarithm puts proportional changes on a comparable scale: higher values indicate more recruits per unit of spawning biomass. The series shows substantial variation among year classes. The 1978, 2008 and 2018 year classes have particularly high recruits-per-spawner values. Following the strong 2018 year class, the ratio declined through the 2022 year class; estimates for 2023–2025 are higher but remain less certain. The spawning-biomass panel generally shows lower ratios at higher biomass, with considerable variation among years at similar biomass. This pattern can reflect density dependence, environmental conditions and estimation uncertainty. Spawning biomass appears in both the horizontal axis and the ratio, which can contribute to the apparent relationship. Model 26.0 uses mean recruitment rather than an estimated Ricker curve. The figure provides a descriptive check on productivity using point estimates of the recruitment-to-biomass ratio.</p>
<p>Biological schedules and selectivity retain their age, sex and year definitions (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-current-biological-schedules">Figure 35</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model262-current-biological-schedules">Table 36</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model262-current-selectivity">Table 37</a>). Fishing mortality is also shown by age (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-fishing-mortality-age">Figure 36</a>). Whole-year spawning exploitation compares paired spawning-biomass calculations from the base model production fit (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-spawn-interval-exploitation">Figure 37</a>). For the interval from spawning in 2026 to spawning in 2027, its production-point estimate is <strong>13.7%</strong>: <strong>3.326 million t</strong> with fishing versus <strong>3.853 million t</strong> without fishing. The branches share prior fishing history and their spawning-date starting population, with 1.375 million t annual catch assumed in 2027. The separate MCMC posterior median for this exploitation fraction is <strong>14.5%</strong>, with a central 95% credible interval of <strong>11.2–18.4%</strong>. These paired-state calculations carry the revised fishery-weight schedule into 2027 and retain the fixed 1.375 million t catch assumption. The production-fit point remains separate from that posterior interval.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.1.2" id="estimated-model-parameters">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="estimated-model-parameters" data-number="6.1.2"><span class="header-section-number">6.1.2</span> Estimated model parameters</h3>
<p>The parameter-family summary identifies fitted parameter groups and their asymptotic uncertainty (<a href="#tbl-model262-current-parameter-families">Table 38</a>). Complete estimates and the largest parameter correlations are retained in <a href="#sec-current-output-appendix">the detailed estimates appendix</a>. The summary likelihood contributions are in <a href="#tbl-model262-current-likelihood-summary">Table 39</a>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.1.3" id="fits-to-the-observations">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="fits-to-the-observations" data-number="6.1.3"><span class="header-section-number">6.1.3</span> Fits to the observations</h3>
<p>The fitted indices follow the main rises and falls in the survey series, including the low ATS biomass in 2006–2009 and its subsequent increase (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-index-fits">Figure 38</a>). Annual departures remain. The BTS residuals include negative departures in 2006 and 2009 and positive departures in 2014–2015, each outside the plotted 95% reference range. The AVO observation in 2015 is also higher than fitted, whereas all ATS biomass residuals fall within that range (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-index-residuals">Figure 39</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model262-index-residual-summary">Table 40</a>). Thus, the broad survey trends are represented more closely than some individual annual observations. BTS residuals account for covariance among survey years. </p>
<p>The fishery selectivity curves show substantial changes in the ages most vulnerable to fishing, with dome-shaped patterns in many years and flatter patterns in others (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-fishery-selectivity-history">Figure 40</a>). BTS selectivity generally increases with age and approaches a plateau, while the ATS curve, shared with AVO, is relatively flat at older ages (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-bts-selectivity-history">Figure 41</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-ats-selectivity-history">Figure 42</a>).  Recruitment varies strongly among years: the 2018 year class, entering at age 1 in 2019, has the largest positive departure from the fitted recruitment level.</p>
<p>The mean-age comparisons show that the model follows most of the observed changes in survey age composition and closely tracks fishery mean age in the domestic period. The clearest sustained fishery discrepancy occurs in the early years, when predicted mean ages are higher than observed (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-observed-predicted-mean-age">Figure 43</a>). The observed bars show plus or minus two standard errors of mean age; they describe sampling uncertainty, rather than uncertainty in the fitted population. Fishery age observations end in 2025. The annual composition panels show how these mean ages arise from the proportions at each age and allow individual cohorts to be followed as they age (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-fishery-cohort-fits-1">Figure 44</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-fishery-cohort-fits-2">Figure 45</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-bts-cohort-fits">Figure 46</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model262-ats-cohort-fits">Figure 47</a>).</p>
<p>Aggregate observed and fitted age proportions agree closely, especially for the fishery, but the residual panels retain patterns by age and year (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-composition-osa">Figure 48</a>; <span class="citation" data-cites="stewart2025osa">Stewart and Monnahan (<a href="#ref-stewart2025osa" role="doc-biblioref">2025</a>)</span>; <span class="citation" data-cites="monnahan2026afscosa">Monnahan et al. (<a href="#ref-monnahan2026afscosa" role="doc-biblioref">2026</a>)</span>). For example, BTS residuals include extended runs of the same sign at several ages, and the early fishery residuals also show structured departures. Averaging across years can obscure these differences. The OSA residual standard deviations are below one for all three sources (about 0.76 for the fishery, 0.86 for BTS and 0.64 for ATS), and the QQ plots are generally narrower than the standard-normal reference, although some BTS tail residuals are large. Close aggregate fits therefore need to be considered alongside the annual patterns. The afscOSA v0.0.1 displays retain the native Model 26.0 OSAs and selected likelihood sample sizes. They describe conditional observation fit under the working-score approximation; parameter uncertainty is outside their scope.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.1.4" id="sec-model260-ats-q-profile">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model260-ats-q-profile" data-number="6.1.4"><span class="header-section-number">6.1.4</span> Profile likelihood diagnostics</h3>
<p>A profile examines how strongly the observations and model assumptions constrain ATS survey catchability in Model 26.0. Catchability scales the survey index relative to the population available to the survey. We fixed this parameter at <strong>17 values from 0.45 to 0.65</strong>, including the freely estimated value of <strong>0.51694</strong>, and re-estimated all other active parameters. The grid uses eight equal intervals on each side of the estimated value: approximately 0.00837 below it and 0.01663 above it. Data, bounds, likelihood terms, and penalties match the Model 26.0 fit, including the updated 2011 and 2013 AVO observations (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-ats-q-profile">Figure 49</a>).</p>
<p>The best fit remains at catchability <strong>0.51694</strong>. Lower or higher values increase the negative log likelihood (NLL), indicating a poorer overall fit after the other parameters have adjusted. The conventional change of 1.92 NLL units is crossed between <strong>0.45000 and 0.45837</strong> on the lower side and between <strong>0.58347 and 0.60010</strong> on the upper side. Linear interpolation between these points gives approximate crossings of <strong>0.4576 and 0.5838</strong>. These are diagnostic bounds from the sampled profile; the objective includes model penalties, and the crossings have been interpolated rather than directly fitted.</p>
<p>The component breakdown shows how the model balances the different data sources. At catchability 0.45, the total NLL increases by <strong>2.48</strong> units. Index likelihoods contribute 2.36 units, while the combined composition fit improves by 0.43 units. The ATS index and compositions fit less well, while BTS compositions fit better. At catchability 0.65, the total increase is <strong>6.80</strong> units. Compositions contribute 4.50 units, largely from the BTS, and selectivity penalties contribute 1.93 units. The combined index term changes by only 0.14 units because improved BTS index fit partly offsets poorer ATS index fit. Thus, the preferred catchability reflects agreement across surveys, fishery observations, and selectivity assumptions.</p>
<p>All 17 fits have maximum absolute gradients below <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> and positive-definite Hessians. Seven points required additional numerical refinement or successful optimizer confirmation. Weighted NLL components sum to the total objective at every point. Scientific evaluation should also consider sensitivity to composition weighting and selectivity assumptions.</p>
<p>The final ATS-q posterior median is <strong>0.5093</strong>, with central 95% credible interval <strong>0.4514–0.5755</strong>. The profile minimum is <strong>0.51694</strong>, with approximate profile limits <strong>0.4576–0.5838</strong>. <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-ats-q-marginal-profile">Figure 50</a> compares the negative log ATS-q marginal density with the optimized profile NLL. The kernel density integrates to one, and each displayed curve is centered at its own minimum over ATS q. The marginal integrates over the other parameters and includes posterior regularization; the profile optimizes those parameters under the native penalized objective. Panel B fits weighted quadratic curves directly to individual-draw native NLL components and compares them with the profile components. All 5,000 draws contribute; binning is excluded. MCMC curves are centered at the ATS-q marginal mode and displayed over the central 99% of sampled q. These conditional mean curves have a different interpretation from the negative log marginal density, which has no unique additive decomposition into the native likelihood terms. The smoothers summarize the broad component trends; tail coverage is limited by the available draws.</p>
<p>The paired MCMC draws show the relationships among ATS q, summed abundance at ages 2–5 in 2026, age-1 abundance in 2019 (the 2018 year class), and projected 2027 female spawning biomass (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-ats-bts-q-ssb2027-pairs">Figure 51</a>). Diagonal panels show their marginal densities. All four quantities are paired within each saved draw.</p>
<p>Projected 2027 female spawning biomass is most strongly associated with the summed abundance of ages 2–5 in 2026 among the quantities shown (<math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.84</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = 0.84</annotation></semantics></math>). This contrasts sharply with the 2024 assessment, in which projected 2025 spawning biomass depended heavily on the estimated magnitude of the 2018 year class (Figure 53 of the 2024 SAFE). The 2018 year-class dependence remains in the projection, as shown by its positive correlation with 2027 spawning biomass (<math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.36</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = 0.36</annotation></semantics></math>), but is less pronounced than the dependence on the younger fish now approaching or contributing to spawning biomass.</p>
<p>At each fixed ATS catchability, we also project 2027 female spawning biomass and its conditional 95% confidence interval (<a href="#tbl-model260-ats-q-ssb2027">Table 41</a>). The projection uses 1,375 kt catch in 2027, mean 2023–2025 fishery selectivity, April 1 spawning, the weight schedules, and the age-15+ group. These conditional profile calculations retain the biological schedules of the fitted assessment.</p>
<p>These intervals propagate fitted-parameter uncertainty using the inverse fixed-q penalized Hessian and the delta method on log spawning biomass. They condition on each ATS q and the stated projection assumptions. They exclude uncertainty in ATS q, future recruitment process variation, and weight-at-age schedules. Thus, they describe uncertainty in the estimated 2027 SSB at each profile point.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.1.5" id="sec-paired-current-retrospectives">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-paired-current-retrospectives" data-number="6.1.5"><span class="header-section-number">6.1.5</span> Retrospective patterns</h3>
<p>Across the full nine peels ending in 2017–2025, Model 26.0 female spawning-biomass Mohn’s rho is <strong>+0.121</strong> (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-catch-revised-mohn-rho">Table 42</a>). Age-1 recruitment rho is <strong>−0.0985</strong>, and maximum fishing-mortality rho is <strong>−0.0636</strong>. Each statistic averages the relative revision between a peel’s terminal estimate and the full-2026 estimate for that same calendar year. The annual revisions are reported in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model260-current-retrospective-revisions">Table 43</a>. </p>
<p>The paired retrospective comparison shows female spawning biomass, age-1 recruitment and maximum fishing mortality for Model 26.0 and the Early-late fishery split Model 26.1.2 sensitivity (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-current-observed-retrospective-trajectories">Figure 52</a>). Each colored curve removes one through nine terminal years and is compared with its own analysis’s full 2026 reference. Model 26.0’s full nine-peel statistics are reported above.</p>
<p>The conditional Model 26.1.2 comparison has nine-peel spawning-biomass rho of <strong>+0.0735</strong>, recruitment rho of <strong>−0.133</strong>, and maximum fishing-mortality rho of <strong>+0.00226</strong>. Both configurations show positive average spawning-biomass revisions and negative average recruitment revisions, while their average fishing-mortality revisions differ. These full-window summaries describe the overall direction of retrospective change across all nine endpoints.</p>
<p>The Model 26.0 simulated-data and posterior-predictive retrospective experiments provide separate conditional comparisons (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-model260-selftest">Section 6.3.1</a>).</p>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="historical-retrospectives">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="historical-retrospectives">Historical retrospectives</h4>
<p>Successive assessments provide different estimates of biomass as observations accumulate and methods change. Following Figure 63 of the 2024 SAFE, <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-historical-retrospectives">Figure 53</a> compares beginning-of-year age-3+ biomass from earlier assessments with the Model 26.0 series. The 2024 comparison uses the published values in the official SAFE Table 27. There was no assessment fit in 2025.</p>
<p>For this historical comparison, age-3+ biomass is the sum of beginning-of-year numbers at ages 3–15+ multiplied by the corresponding fishery weights at age in each year. This definition differs from total population-weight biomass reported elsewhere in the assessment.</p>
<p>The 2026 assessment estimates age-3+ biomass in 2023 at 11.983 million t, compared with 9.695 million t in the 2024 assessment, an increase of about 24%. The corresponding estimates for 2024 are 10.185 and 9.415 million t, a difference of about 8.2%. The Model 26.0 trajectory declines from 14.438 million t in 2022 to 8.774 million t in 2025, then rises to 13.286 million t in 2026. Earlier assessment trajectories show that both the magnitude and timing of biomass changes have been revised over time.</p>
<p>These historical comparisons combine the effects of new observations, revised biological inputs and changes in model structure. The retrospective peels above instead remove recent years within a specified model framework. The historical figure is therefore a record of assessment revisions, with each series retaining its original assumptions and available years.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.1.6" id="sec-francis-comparison">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-francis-comparison" data-number="6.1.6"><span class="header-section-number">6.1.6</span> Age-composition weighting comparison</h3>
<p>The age-composition diagnostics suggest relatively minor changes to the weights used in the 2026 assessment (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-francis-sample-size-comparison">Figure 54</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-francis-mean-age-residuals">Figure 55</a>). Given the small suggested adjustments, the 2023–2025 fishery age compositions therefore retain input information weights of 443, 578 and 530. These weights determine the influence of the compositions in model fitting. The data section reports the raw numbers of fish sampled.</p>
<p>Composition weighting can be evaluated more fully in future assessments, including alternatives such as the Dirichlet-multinomial distribution, which allows greater variation among age samples than the multinomial model. Such comparisons would help assess whether estimating this additional variation within the model improves the treatment of age-composition data and changes the resulting stock estimates.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="6.2" id="sec-model261-results">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model261-results" data-number="6.2"><span class="header-section-number">6.2</span> Model 26.1 split-fishery alternatives</h2>
<p>Models 26.1.0 and 26.1.1 separate the Foreign fishery through 1990 from the Modern domestic fishery beginning in 1991. Their annual selectivity standard deviations are fixed at 0.5, while the declining-age penalty is 12.5 in Model 26.1.0 and 3.125 in Model 26.1.1. The zero-penalty case provides a further comparison. The Model 26.1.2 sensitivity shown here retains the 3.125 penalty and fixes the Foreign and Modern annual process standard deviations at 0.1235 and 0.582, respectively. The remaining parameters and annual selectivity effects are estimated conditionally on these values.</p>
<p>The likelihood comparison separates data-likelihood contributions, penalty terms and the marginal fitting criterion (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-model261-nll-comparison">Table 44</a>). The projections use the revised ordinary fits and the Early-late fishery split Model 26.1.2 comparison. The alternatives retain matched observations, likelihood weights and projection assumptions (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-coordinated-model-abc">Table 45</a>).</p>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.2.1" id="selectivity">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="selectivity" data-number="6.2.1"><span class="header-section-number">6.2.1</span> Selectivity</h3>
<p>Separating the Foreign (1964–1990) and Modern domestic (1991–2026) fisheries changes the fitted selectivity most visibly near the boundary between the two periods. Over much of the later period, Models 26.0 and 26.1.0 retain similar annual age patterns, including the peaks and declines at older ages (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model261-selectivity-history">Figure 56</a>). The split allows the Foreign curve to differ more freely from the Modern curve, while Model 26.0 represents the history as a single fishery.</p>
<p>Both models estimate a shift from 1990 to 1991 toward lower relative selectivity at younger ages and higher relative selectivity at ages 11 and older. The shift is larger in Model 26.1.0: at age 5, the change is about −0.69 on the native mean-one scale, compared with −0.31 in Model 26.0; at ages 12 and older, the increases are about 0.55 and 0.24, respectively (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model261-selectivity-boundary">Figure 57</a>). This comparison shows how the split changes the estimated transition. The fitted curves alone establish neither an abrupt change in fishing practices nor an improvement in the population estimates; the observation fits and retrospective results provide the complementary checks below.</p>
<p>The full-history curves are divided by each year’s maximum so that their shapes can be compared. The boundary-year display instead retains native mean-one normalization, and its differences refer to that scale. These are fitted point curves. The Model 26.1.2 curves used in subsequent comparisons retain the fitted selectivity states from its fixed-SD conditional fit and remain distinct from the Model 26.1.0 comparison here.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.2.2" id="sec-fishery-composition-comparison">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-fishery-composition-comparison" data-number="6.2.2"><span class="header-section-number">6.2.2</span> Fishery age-composition fits</h3>
<p>We compared Models 26.0 and 26.1.2 using the same 62 annual fishery age compositions and likelihood weights (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-fishery-fit-comparison">Figure 58</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model2612-fishery-fit-comparison">Figure 59</a>). Model 26.0 fitted one fishery across the full record; Model 26.1.2 separated the Foreign fishery through 1990 from the Modern domestic fishery beginning in 1991. We displayed both models over those same periods to compare their fits directly. Both models reproduced the dominant age groups in the combined compositions, while the annual plots revealed differences that the combined summaries obscured.</p>
<p>Model 26.1.2 fitted the Modern domestic observations more closely. It reduced the sample-weighted root-mean-square difference in age proportions from <strong>0.693 to 0.590 percentage points</strong> and the root-mean-square error in annual mean age from <strong>0.123 to 0.0963 years</strong>. Both models predicted a younger mean age than the observations showed in 1991, but Model 26.1.2 reduced that discrepancy from <strong>0.510 to 0.339 years</strong>. The smaller differences across ages and years showed that the split-fishery configuration improved the modern fit rather than simply matching its combined age distribution.</p>
<p>Model 26.0 fitted the Foreign-period observations more closely. Model 26.1.2 increased the sample-weighted age-proportion error from <strong>2.67 to 3.43 percentage points</strong> and the annual mean-age error from <strong>0.655 to 0.696 years</strong>. Both models predicted older mean ages than the early observations showed, particularly in 1964–1965 and 1970. The age-by-year panels showed persistent overprediction at several older ages and underprediction at younger ages during much of the early record. Separating the fisheries therefore improved the modern fit while leaving larger discrepancies in the Foreign period.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="6.3" id="sec-evaluation">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-evaluation" data-number="6.3"><span class="header-section-number">6.3</span> Further model evaluations</h2>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.3.1" id="sec-model260-selftest">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model260-selftest" data-number="6.3.1"><span class="header-section-number">6.3.1</span> Observation-error retrospective self-test</h3>
<p>In response to Plan Team and SSC requests to investigate retrospective patterns, we developed a new simulation-based retrospective experiment for this assessment (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-current-simulation-retrospective-revisions">Figure 60</a>). Its distinctive feature is a paired design that examines revisions both at the fitted parameter estimates and across plausible parameter states from the regularized posterior. One set of ten simulated datasets uses the fitted parameters; a second set uses ten posterior parameter draws. Each dataset has its own full 2026 fit and nine optimization peels ending in 2017–2025. Revisions compare each peel’s terminal estimate with its own full fit for the same calendar year. This approach extends the usual retrospective analysis by examining how observation variation and uncertainty in the generating parameters influence the revisions, providing additional context for interpreting the assessment’s retrospective pattern.</p>
<p>Across all nine peels ending in 2017–2025, Model 26.0 assessment Mohn’s rho for female spawning biomass is <strong>+0.121</strong>, compared with median values of <strong>−0.0117</strong> for datasets generated at the fitted parameters and <strong>−0.0574</strong> for datasets generated from posterior draws. The assessment value exceeds every simulated rho in both sets: the fixed-parameter range is <strong>−0.115 to +0.0335</strong>, and the posterior-draw range is <strong>−0.0971 to +0.116</strong>. Thus, the positive average spawning-biomass revision in the assessment is stronger than that reproduced by these simulated datasets.</p>
<p>For age-1 recruitment, the assessment’s nine-peel rho is <strong>−0.0985</strong>, within both simulated ranges. Median recruitment rho is <strong>−0.00751</strong> in the fixed-parameter set and <strong>+0.0830</strong> in the posterior-draw set. The contrast between spawning biomass and recruitment shows that the retrospective pattern depends on the population quantity considered.</p>
<p>The paired design explores how observation variation and uncertainty in generating parameters contribute to the full nine-peel pattern. Ten datasets per branch provide an exploratory comparison. The technical supplement describes the fixed process history, data-generation approximations and other conditioning assumptions. These experiments assess biomass and recruitment revisions. Confidence bands describing retrospective ABC or OFL patterns are beyond the scope of this work but would be interesting to evaluate.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="6.3.2" id="sec-model260-posterior-review">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-model260-posterior-review" data-number="6.3.2"><span class="header-section-number">6.3.2</span> Posterior diagnostics and predictive checks</h3>
<p>The regularized posterior explores parameter uncertainty separately from the production base-model estimates (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-snuts-pairs">Figure 61</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-snuts-uncertainty">Figure 62</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-snuts-marginals">Figure 63</a>). Four chains each retained 1,250 draws after 1,000 warmup iterations. Combined parameter diagnostics give maximum R-hat 1.024 and minimum bulk ESS 242, with zero divergences and zero maximum-treedepth events. The reported population quantities mix more consistently: maximum R-hat is 1.0013 and minimum bulk ESS is 3,914. MCMC standard errors of the 2026 spawning-biomass and biomass means are about 4,110 t and 20,600 t; their first-half versus second-half mean shifts are less than 0.03 posterior standard deviations. These diagnostics describe the saved chains and retain the parameter-level qualifications.</p>
<section class="level4 unnumbered" id="final-posterior-summaries">
<h4 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="final-posterior-summaries">Final posterior summaries</h4>
<p>The posterior mean female spawning biomass in 2026 is 2.965 million t, with a central 95% credible interval of 2.450–3.584 million t (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-catch-revised-posterior-check">Table 46</a>). These summaries use all 5,000 retained MCMC draws under the regularizing priors and fixed biological inputs. Full-precision results are downloadable as CSV files containing terminal stock and selectivity summaries (CSV), annual population intervals (CSV), summaries of all 1,266 parameters (CSV), and spawning-exploitation intervals (CSV).</p>
<p>Predictive checks ask whether the fitted model can generate data that resemble the observations (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-index-ppc">Figure 64</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-model260-composition-ppc">Figure 65</a>). We selected 1,000 MCMC draws spanning the four chains. Each draw supplies a possible set of model parameters, from which a new set of observations is simulated. The shaded ranges therefore include both parameter uncertainty and the sampling variation assumed by the model. Points outside these ranges, or repeated patterns of differences, help identify features the model struggles to reproduce. The ranges apply to each age or year individually; some points outside them are expected even when the assumptions are appropriate.</p>
<p>For the indices, simulated observations use the same error assumptions used in fitting, including the relationships among BTS errors. The overall BTS mismatch measure is as large as the observed measure in only 0.2% of the simulations, indicating that this feature of the BTS data is rarely reproduced. Normal error assumptions also allow some simulated indices to be negative.</p>
<p>For age compositions, simulated fish are randomly assigned to age groups using each draw’s predicted proportions and the sample size used in fitting, rounded to a whole number. The simulations approximate the fitting method, which adds a small constant (0.001) to age proportions. The figure compares the latest three actual samples for each source with these simulated age proportions. Age conversions, weights and other biological inputs are held fixed. These checks assess how well the model reproduces observations; the retrospective analyses address how estimates change as additional years of data become available.</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="7" id="sec-projections">
<h1 data-number="7"><span class="header-section-number">7</span> Projections and harvest recommendations</h1>
<section class="level2" data-number="7.1" id="proposed-tier-3-configuration-and-reference-points">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="proposed-tier-3-configuration-and-reference-points" data-number="7.1"><span class="header-section-number">7.1</span> Proposed Tier 3 configuration and reference points</h2>
<p>The proposed fishery selectivity is the mean of the 2023–2025 annual curves, the latest three years with fishery age observations. Each age is averaged before scaling the resulting curve to a maximum of one. The separately inferred 2026 curve is distinguished from directly age-informed years (<a href="#sec-proposed-projection-input-curves">the projection-input appendix</a>).</p>
<p>The deterministic recruitment level uses the arithmetic mean of age-1 entries in 1978–2023, corresponding to birth cohorts 1977–2022. The less precise 2024–2026 entries are excluded. Every entry in the advice tables equals this selected historical mean. The separate projection figures add future recruitment variation to illustrate a range of possible paths. Reference points and fishing rates are reported in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-proposed-tier3-reference-points">Table 47</a>. The Model 26.1.2 column uses the revised Early-late fishery split comparison under the same projection assumptions.</p>
<p>The Tier 3 reference points are spawning-potential quantities. The ABC rule reduces fishing mortality below B40% and sets it to zero below B20%. Projections start from each fitted population and use the stated catch scenarios and biological inputs. The author-rate fraction is one, subject to the risk evaluation and final review.</p>
<p>The previous-year OFL-equivalent fishing mortality is reported in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-prior-year-ofl-f">Section 10</a>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="7.2" id="standard-harvest-scenarios">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="standard-harvest-scenarios" data-number="7.2"><span class="header-section-number">7.2</span> Standard harvest scenarios</h2>
<p>The proposed projections retain the standard harvest scenarios and their common biology (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-proposed-tier3-scenarios">Table 48</a>). The expected-catch scenario assumes 1.375 million t in each of 2027 and 2028; the 2028 catch is a planning assumption. Short-term outputs are reported in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-proposed-tier3-short-term">Table 49</a>.</p>
<p>The catch and female spawning-biomass panels compare Alternative 2 with recent-mean-F Alternative 3 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-proposed-tier3-catch">Figure 66</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-proposed-tier3-ssb">Figure 67</a>). Black lines show the means of 1,000 future-recruitment simulations, ribbons show their 5th–95th percentiles, and ten colored trajectories illustrate individual outcomes. Each color follows the same recruitment realization across both alternatives and figures. Recruitment follows the established inverse-Gaussian method, using the arithmetic and harmonic means of the fitted 1978–2023 age-1 entries. Initial age-1 abundance in 2027 equals the historical arithmetic mean; each subsequent entry varies among simulations. The widening bands show how future recruitment variation accumulates as new cohorts enter the fishery and spawning population. Alternative 2 catch paths coincide in 2027 and 2028 because those catches are prescribed.</p>
<p>The projection tables retain all seven scenarios with recruitment fixed at the historical arithmetic mean (<a href="#tbl-proposed-tier3-catch">Table 50</a>; <a href="#tbl-proposed-tier3-ssb">Table 51</a>; <a href="#tbl-proposed-tier3-f">Table 52</a>). The historical phase plot places the fitted 1981–2026 trajectory and deterministic Alternative 2 projections for 2027–2028 on common axes (<a href="#fig-proposed-tier3-phase">Figure 68</a>). The horizontal axis is female spawning biomass divided by B35%; the vertical axis is maximum fishing mortality at age divided by F35%. Both denominators are the current primary projection reference points (B35% = 2.155 million t; F35% = 0.658 per year), held constant across the trajectory. This common benchmark shows changes in the fitted stock and fishing mortality through time. The 2024 assessment used annually varying reference points; the historical positions here therefore also reflect the choice of a common current benchmark. F35% is a spawning-per-recruit proxy for FMSY, and B35% is the corresponding spawning-biomass reference point. Solid lines mark ratios of one, and the dashed vertical line marks half B35%. Two-digit year labels trace the trajectory, with the two projection years boxed and shaded yellow. The fitted 2026 position and both projected positions are above B35% and below F35%. </p>
<section class="level3" data-number="7.2.1" id="sec-catch-decision-probabilities">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-catch-decision-probabilities" data-number="7.2.1"><span class="header-section-number">7.2.1</span> Decision table</h3>
<p>As in past assessments, we present estimated consequences and probabilities for a range of future catches and the subsequent fishing effort implied by each choice (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-current-decision-definitions">Table 53</a>; <a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-current-decision-model26">Table 54</a>). The decision table compares eight possible 2027 catches, from 10 to 2,540 kt, using Model 26.0 with the updated AVO data. The indicator definitions identify the quantities, comparison benchmarks and years used in the calculations. Together, the tables show how catch choices affect fishing mortality, future spawning biomass and age structure, and how likely each choice is to meet the specified benchmarks.</p>
<p>Each catch column represents a different fishing strategy. Fishing mortality is calculated to achieve that catch in 2027, then held constant through 2031. Catches in subsequent years therefore change with the projected abundance and age composition of the stock. The effort indicator gives the probability that mean age-specific fishing mortality in 2027 exceeds its 2026 value. Interpreting it as relative effort assumes that catchability and the age pattern of fishery selectivity remain fixed. It provides a comparison among strategies rather than a forecast of vessel numbers, fishing days or operating costs.</p>
<p>Readers can compare columns to examine the trade-off between the initial catch and subsequent stock conditions. The probability rows summarize the chance of crossing the stated biomass, fishing-mortality or age-structure benchmarks. These are conditional comparisons that support catch decisions alongside the standard harvest projections and risk table.</p>
<p>Entries are approximate chances out of 100. They propagate uncertainty in the fitted population, selectivity, estimated mean recruitment and comparison benchmarks. Future recruitment is held at the estimated 1978–2023 mean, and biological schedules are fixed. These probabilities describe uncertainty in the assessment estimates under each catch choice. Additional year-to-year recruitment variation and uncertainty in weights and maturity are outside these calculations. Values displayed as 0 or 100 reflect rounding.</p>
<p>The 1,270-kt column is retained for comparison with the earlier decision-table analysis. The expected-catch scenario elsewhere in this section assumes 1,375 kt in 2027 and 2028. The decision tables provide a broader comparison of catch choices; they use local asymptotic uncertainty rather than MCMC draws.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" data-number="7.2.2" id="sec-projection-selectivity-sensitivity">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-projection-selectivity-sensitivity" data-number="7.2.2"><span class="header-section-number">7.2.2</span> Reference point sensitivity to fishery selectivity specification</h3>
<p>Fishery selectivity determines how fishing mortality is distributed across ages and therefore affects both the reference fishing rates and the catches obtained at those rates. The central projection uses the age-specific arithmetic mean of the raw 2023–2025 fishery selectivity curves, rescaled so that its maximum is one. This recent three-year average smooths annual variation while retaining the age pattern from the latest years with fishery age observations. Averaging precedes rescaling because normalizing each annual curve first would give a different average. <a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-projection-selectivity-recent">Figure 69</a> introduces this recent-average specification and contrasts it with individual annual estimates. The inferred 2026 curve is shown separately because fishery age observations end in 2025. It provides a terminal-year comparison, while the management projections retain the 2023–2025 average.</p>
<p>The recent curves show that changes in fishery recruitment involve particular ages rather than a uniform shift toward younger fish. The first ascending half-maximum crossing was near age 6 in 2021–2022, compared with approximately 4.5, 5.0 and 5.2 in 2023–2025. Relative selectivity at age 5 was especially high in 2023 and then declined in 2024–2025. Selectivity at ages 1–3 remained low and varied independently. These differences matter because a curve that exposes age-5 fish more strongly can produce a different catch and spawning impact from one that concentrates fishing at older ages, even when both have the same maximum selectivity.</p>
<p>The full annual comparisons show which parts of each curve differ from the projection assumption (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-projection-selectivity-annual">Figure 70</a>). The repeated 2023–2025 reference makes shifts in the ascending limb, peak and older-age tail visible across 2007–2026. For example, the 2019 curve peaks near age 7 and declines substantially at older ages, whereas several earlier curves retain high selectivity across the older ages. Thus, the annual panels provide the age-specific explanation for the management differences in the next figure. The older curves represent alternative fishing patterns for sensitivity analysis. Their relevance as forecasts depends on evidence about current and future fishery conditions.</p>
<p>Annual selectivity alternatives give both higher and lower catch ceilings than the recent-average baseline (<a href="#fig-projection-selectivity-effects">Figure 71</a>). Of the twenty curves, 14 produce a higher maximum ABC in 2027 and 12 do so in 2028. Changes range from -8.2% to +12.0% in 2027 and from -5.9% to +8.4% in 2028. These are conditional sensitivities under common population, recruitment, biological and catch assumptions.</p>
<p>The lowest annual-curve maximum ABC occurs with the 2018 curve in 2027 and the 2019 curve in 2028. The 2025 curve changes the ceilings by +1.5% and -4.4%, respectively. The age pattern affects immediate catches and the ages surviving into the following year. F40% and F35% are recalculated for each curve; the assumed catch remains 1.375 million t in each year.</p>
<p>The younger-age summaries explain why a single description such as “younger selection” is insufficient (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-projection-selectivity-trends">Figure 72</a>). They separate exposure of ages 1–3, selectivity at ages 4 and 5, the first ascending half-maximum age, and changes across the full curve. For example, from 2022 to 2023 the half-maximum age falls from about 6.0 to 4.5 years, while the curve-weighted mean age changes only from 10.09 to 10.00 years. Conversely, from 2023 to 2025 the half-maximum age rises while the curve-weighted mean age falls. The ascending limb and older-age tail therefore move in different directions. This figure connects the detailed annual panels to the reference-point results: the age at which fish begin entering the fishery and the relative exposure of older fish carry different information. Its mean-age measure weights selectivity equally across model ages 1–15, with age 15 representing the plus group; population abundance and catch composition are excluded from that shape index.</p>
<p>The reference-rate comparison makes the dependence on age selection explicit (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-selectivity-f35-mean-age">Figure 73</a>). Under fixed biology, each curve has its own fully selected F35% rate, the fishing-mortality scalar that reduces lifetime spawning output per recruit to 35% of the unfished level. Later exposure can allow more spawning before capture and therefore support a higher fully selected rate at the same spawning-per-recruit target. However, the full curve, including its older-age tail, determines this response. The high 2019 F35% illustrates how a reference scalar can rise sharply under a particular age pattern. Such an increase describes the rate permitted under that pattern; it provides no independent evidence of increased stock productivity or a larger sustainable catch.</p>
<p>Two distinctions are essential when interpreting an FMSY proxy against selected age. First, F35% is a spawning-per-recruit proxy for FMSY, whereas FMSY itself depends on the equilibrium yield and recruitment relationship. The historical FMSY comparison and this F35% diagnostic therefore represent different reference quantities. Second, fully selected F is a scalar: fishing mortality at each age equals that scalar multiplied by selectivity at that age. Comparisons among years require the same selectivity normalization and the corresponding age-specific mortality pattern. The scatterplot uses a selectivity-weighted age index over ages 1–10, whereas its spawning-per-recruit calculation includes ages 1–14 and 15+, fixed natural mortality, maturity and the selected projection spawning weights, and quarter-year spawning timing. Its age index also differs from the ages 1–15 index in the preceding figure and from the abundance-weighted age of selected fish. It is a compact descriptor of curve shape, and a common mean selected age can accompany different reference rates. The complete selectivity curve and resulting catch and spawning effects provide the appropriate basis for interpreting the FMSY proxy and comparing harvest specifications.</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="8" id="sec-risk-table-abc">
<h1 data-number="8"><span class="header-section-number">8</span> Risk table and ABC recommendation</h1>
<p>The author risk evaluation retains all four categories at <strong>Level 1 – Normal</strong> (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#tbl-risk-summary">Table 55</a>). The ecosystem and fishery observations are summarized below. Working recommendations remain subject to author scientific evaluation and Plan Team, SSC and Council review. The Level 1 evaluation supports no reduction from maximum permissible ABC.</p>

<section class="level2" data-number="8.1" id="sec-risk-assessment">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-risk-assessment" data-number="8.1"><span class="header-section-number">8.1</span> Assessment-related considerations</h2>
<p>Model 26.0 (Rceattle) is the adopted assessment model and main proposal for Tier 3 calculations and specifications. The alternative models examine how the assessment responds to changes in its structure and treatment of annual selectivity variation. Comparisons with Models 23.0 and 23.2 connect the current assessment to the previous formulation and help distinguish the effects of updated observations from changes in model structure. The split-fishery alternatives test whether separate selectivity patterns for the Foreign fishery in 1964–1990 and the Modern domestic fishery from 1991 onward better represent the fishing history. Further comparisons vary the constraint on declining selectivity and the treatment of year-to-year changes in selectivity.</p>
<p>Model 26.1.2 provides the principal sensitivity to these choices. Its underlying marginal formulation estimates the variability of Modern fishery selectivity while accounting for annual selectivity effects. The conditional comparison presented here fixes the Foreign and Modern process standard deviations at their selected full-data values and estimates the remaining parameters and annual selectivity effects. This configuration fits the Modern fishery age compositions more closely than Model 26.0, while larger discrepancies remain in the Foreign period. The result identifies a potential benefit of separating the fisheries, alongside a trade-off in how the model represents the earlier observations.</p>
<p>The Model 26.1.2 retrospective analysis asks whether estimates change as the most recent observations are successively removed. Each shortened-data fit holds the process standard deviations fixed and is compared with a full-data fit using the same conditional estimation method. This matching reference makes the retrospective differences interpretable within the fixed-SD configuration. The diagnostic therefore describes stability when the assumed magnitude of annual selectivity variation is held constant. Re-estimating that variation in each shortened dataset could change the retrospective pattern, and uncertainty in the process standard deviations remains outside this comparison. Improved fits to the Modern observations consequently provide one part of the model evaluation; broader retrospective reliability requires evidence across the relevant estimation choices. Model 26.0 remains the basis for the Tier 3 specifications, with Model 26.1.2 used to assess sensitivity to fishery structure and selectivity assumptions.</p>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="8.2" id="population-dynamics-risk-summary">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="population-dynamics-risk-summary" data-number="8.2"><span class="header-section-number">8.2</span> Population dynamics risk summary</h2>
<p>Population dynamics risk is <strong>Level 1 – Normal</strong>. Cold spring conditions coincided with low egg and larval abundance; temperature-dependent timing complicates interpretation of these early-life indices. Southeastern Bering Sea (SEBS) age-0 abundance was also low. Above-average late-summer large copepod abundance, lipid-rich copepods and euphausiids, and above-average SEBS age-0 energy density indicate favorable feeding and potential survival through the first winter. Northern Bering Sea (NBS) age-0 energy density was below average, while adult-pollock cannibalism was low overall; age-1 specificity remains unverified. The regional contrasts and supporting evidence are described in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-ecosystem-population-dynamics">Section 11.1</a> within <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-ecosystem-considerations">Section 11</a>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="8.3" id="environmental-and-ecosystem-risk-summary">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="environmental-and-ecosystem-risk-summary" data-number="8.3"><span class="header-section-number">8.3</span> Environmental and ecosystem risk summary</h2>
<p>The environmental and ecosystem synthesis supports a <strong>Level 1 – Normal</strong> ecosystem score. Following the warm period of 2014–2021 and near-average thermal conditions in 2022–2025, the EBS shelf shifted to cool conditions in 2026. The expanded cold pool, abundant lipid-rich prey and improving adult condition provide favorable context for juvenile and adult pollock. Increased pollock biomass may increase competition; prey and condition indicators suggest adequate food, while the effects of increasing sablefish abundance remain a research question. <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-ecosystem-considerations">Section 11</a> presents the detailed distribution, environmental, prey, competitor and predator evidence, including conditions for later juveniles and adults in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-ecosystem-juveniles-adults">Section 11.2</a>. These category scores support the recommendation for no reduction from maximum permissible ABC.</p>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="8.4" id="sec-risk-fishery">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-risk-fishery" data-number="8.4"><span class="header-section-number">8.4</span> Fishery-informed Stock Considerations</h2>
<p>Fishing conditions differed between the two seasons. The observer data indicate that A-season fishing in 2026 appeared good. Later in the B-season, fishing occurred farther north than normal, and pollock of desirable sizes were limited. The late-season observations therefore qualify the favorable A-season picture and identify changes in where fishing occurred and the sizes available to the fishery.</p>
<p>We retain the <strong>Level 1 – Normal</strong> score for fishery-informed stock considerations. This score reflects the author’s qualitative assessment of fishing conditions across the year. The observations provide context for interpreting fishery performance; their implications for stock-wide abundance remain uncertain. A standardized comparison of fishing locations, effort and size composition would help distinguish changes in fishery availability from changes in overall stock abundance.</p>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="8.5" id="ecosystem-and-socioeconomic-profile-development">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="ecosystem-and-socioeconomic-profile-development" data-number="8.5"><span class="header-section-number">8.5</span> Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile development</h2>
<p>Development of the EBS pollock Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) continues alongside the assessment <span class="citation" data-cites="shotwell2026pollockesp">(<a href="#ref-shotwell2026pollockesp" role="doc-biblioref">Shotwell et al. 2026</a>)</span>. The archived September 2026 development report supplies exploratory background, and the AI-assisted draft appears as <a href="#sec-esp-2026-appendix">Appendix B</a>. The 2026 Eastern Bering Sea Ecosystem Status Report describes an external Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM) analysis that identified <strong>sea ice extent</strong>, <strong>sea surface temperature (SST)</strong> and <strong>summer large copepods</strong> as indicators with statistically supported relationships to age-1 recruitment <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>. The exploratory Rceattle DSEM pilot in the appendix uses late-summer SST and cold-pool extent as two environmental proxies. Its scope supports a separate assessment of those proxies. Evaluating all three external relationships within Rceattle requires additional testing.</p>
<p>The first application of DSEM has been completed as a draft in the <a href="#sec-esp-2026-appendix">ESP draft</a>. Development and implementation of an integrated version within Rceattle continue from the work presented in the September 2026 development document <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2026developments">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2026developments" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2026</a>)</span>. We see the Ecosystem Status Report (ESR), the ESP, and integration of ecosystem information within the full assessment model as logical applications of ecosystem-based methods for providing informed catch advice to the Council.</p>
<p>Since all four categories are Level 1 – Normal, we recommend no reduction from maximum permissible ABC.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="9" id="sec-status-determination">
<h1 data-number="9"><span class="header-section-number">9</span> Status determination</h1>
<p>Under the Magnuson–Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, stock status is evaluated for overfishing, an overfished condition, and the risk of approaching an overfished condition.</p><p>For Tier 3, B35% is the BMSY proxy. MSST is evaluated using the biomass and projection tests below. Alternative 6 fishes at the OFL rate in every projected year. Alternative 7 fishes at the maximum-ABC rate in 2027–2028 and the OFL rate from 2029 onward.</p><p>Overfishing in 2025. Catch of 1,326,215.61 t was below the specified Bering Sea subarea OFL of 2,957,000 t. Thus, the stock was not subjected to overfishing in 2025.</p><p>Overfished in 2026. Biomass below half B35% indicates an overfished condition; biomass above B35% indicates the stock is above MSST. Between those levels, status depends on Alternative 6 biomass in 2036: below B35% indicates an overfished condition; otherwise, the stock is above MSST. Current biomass is 3.057 million t for Model 26.0 and 3.065 million t for the Early-late fishery split Model 26.1.2 sensitivity, above their respective B35% values of 2.155 and 2.177 million t. Both therefore indicate the stock is not overfished; the 2036 test is unnecessary.</p><p>Approaching an overfished condition. Under Alternative 7, 2028 biomass below half B35% indicates an approaching overfished condition; biomass above B35% indicates it is not approaching that condition. If that biomass falls between half B35% and B35%, use Alternative 7 biomass in 2038 for the long-term test. Biomass below B35% in that long-term test indicates an approaching overfished condition. Projected 2028 biomass is 3.123 million t for Model 26.0 and 3.179 million t for Model 26.1.2, both above B35%. Neither model indicates an approaching overfished condition; the 2038 test is unnecessary.</p><p>These comparisons use deterministic historical-mean recruitment. Assessment conclusions and adopted catch specifications remain separate from final NMFS status determinations.</p><div id="status-model-options">
