</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="10" id="sec-prior-year-ofl-f">
<h1 data-number="10"><span class="header-section-number">10</span> F limit</h1>
<p>Following section 4.15 of the assessment guidelines, F limit is reverse-engineered as the annual fishing mortality that would have produced the previous year’s OFL using the recommended model’s estimated population for that year. For this 2026 assessment, the calculation therefore uses the adopted <strong>2025 Bering Sea pollock OFL of 2.957 million t</strong> (<span class="citation" data-cites="noaa2025bsaifinalspecs">National Marine Fisheries Service (<a href="#ref-noaa2025bsaifinalspecs" role="doc-biblioref">2025</a>)</span>) and the Model 26.0 beginning-of-year 2025 numbers at age, fishery weights, natural mortality and realized selectivity.</p>
<p>Solving the annual Baranov catch equation gives <strong>F limit = 0.787 per year</strong> on the maximum-F-across-ages scale used in this report, with the maximum at age 6. The equivalent scalar on Rceattle’s native mean-normalized selectivity scale is <strong>0.439 per year</strong>. Both scalings give the same fishing mortality at age and reproduce the adopted 2025 OFL. This calculation holds the fitted population and biological inputs fixed while changing fishing mortality.</p>
<p>The calculation finds the value of <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\mathrm{limit}}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying</p>
<p><span id="eq-flimit-2025"><math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mn>2025</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2025</mn></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2025</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2025</mn></mrow><mo>*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2025</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2025</mn></mrow><mo>*</mo></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="true">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="true">{</mo><mi>−</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2025</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2025</mn></mrow><mo>*</mo></msubsup><mo form="postfix" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo form="postfix" stretchy="true">}</mo></mrow><mo form="postfix" stretchy="true">]</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
C^{\mathrm{OFL}}_{2025}=
\sum_{a=1}^{15+} N_{a,2025}\,w^{\mathrm{fishery}}_{a,2025}
\frac{F_{\mathrm{limit}}\,s^{*}_{a,2025}}
{M_{a,2025}+F_{\mathrm{limit}}\,s^{*}_{a,2025}}
\left[1-\exp\!\left\{-\left(M_{a,2025}+F_{\mathrm{limit}}\,s^{*}_{a,2025}\right)\right\}\right].
 \qquad(1)</annotation></semantics></math></span></p>
<p>Here <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is beginning-of-year abundance, <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><msup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{\mathrm{fishery}}</annotation></semantics></math> is fishery weight-at-age, <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is annual natural mortality, and <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>*</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is the fitted selectivity curve rescaled to a maximum of one. Thus <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\mathrm{limit}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the maximum annual fishing mortality across ages. The sum includes ages 1–15+. Abundance in millions of fish and weight in kg give catch in thousand tons.</p>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="11" id="sec-ecosystem-considerations">
<h1 data-number="11"><span class="header-section-number">11</span> Ecosystem considerations</h1>
<p>A draft Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) is presented in <a href="#sec-esp-2026-appendix">Appendix B</a>. It brings together indicators of pollock habitat, food-web conditions and fishery performance to provide context for the assessment. The ESP complements the population model by organizing evidence about processes that can affect year-class strength, fish growth and the distribution of fish available to surveys and the fishery. This broader perspective helps interpret changes in abundance and age composition alongside the environmental conditions experienced by successive cohorts.</p>
<p>The draft 2026 Eastern Bering Sea Ecosystem Status Report provides the environmental and food-web evidence summarized here <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>. In 2026, cool spring conditions and an extensive cold pool coincided with low egg, larval and southeastern Bering Sea age-0 abundance. At the same time, favorable zooplankton abundance and lipid content, together with above-average southeastern Bering Sea age-0 energy density, indicated good feeding conditions for surviving juveniles. These contrasting signals emphasize the importance of timing, region and life stage: low early abundance and favorable later feeding conditions can occur within the same year. Their implications for recruitment depend on survival through the subsequent winter and later juvenile stages.</p>
<p>The following subsections connect these observations to pollock population processes. The first considers environmental conditions, prey, competitors and predators affecting eggs, larvae and early juveniles. The second addresses the distribution, feeding conditions and condition of later juveniles and adults, including how temperature and vertical habitat use can affect survey availability. Together, these indicators help distinguish changes in population abundance from changes in where fish occur and how effectively surveys sample them. The synthesis informs interpretation of the assessment and the risk-category evaluation summarized in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-risk-table-abc">Section 8</a>; the individual indicators provide complementary evidence rather than a direct forecast of recruitment or an automatic adjustment to catch advice.</p>
<section class="level2" data-number="11.1" id="sec-ecosystem-population-dynamics">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-ecosystem-population-dynamics" data-number="11.1"><span class="header-section-number">11.1</span> Ecosystem impacts of EBS pollock population dynamics</h2>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="environmental-processes">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="environmental-processes">Environmental Processes</h3>
<p>A very weak winter Aleutian Low in 2025/2026 brought cool Arctic air across the EBS <span class="citation" data-cites="lemagiewang2026atmosphere">(<a href="#ref-lemagiewang2026atmosphere" role="doc-biblioref">Lemagie and Wang 2026</a>)</span>. <strong>Sea ice extent</strong> remained above average for six weeks during March–April 2026 <span class="citation" data-cites="thoman2026seaice">(<a href="#ref-thoman2026seaice" role="doc-biblioref">Thoman 2026</a>)</span>. The resulting 2°C cold pool was approximately 150% larger than in 2025 and the fifth-largest during 1982–2026; the 0°C cold pool was the largest since 2013 <span class="citation" data-cites="rohanbarnett2026coldpool">(<a href="#ref-rohanbarnett2026coldpool" role="doc-biblioref">Rohan and Barnett 2026</a>)</span>. <strong>Sea surface temperatures</strong> in the SEBS were colder than in 2025, especially during January–April, and remained below average for most of the year <span class="citation" data-cites="lemagiecallahan2026sst">(<a href="#ref-lemagiecallahan2026sst" role="doc-biblioref">Lemagie and Callahan 2026</a>)</span>. In May 2026, spring winds favored Ekman transport off the shelf, influencing larval dispersal trajectories <span class="citation" data-cites="hennon2026transport">(<a href="#ref-hennon2026transport" role="doc-biblioref">Hennon 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="prey">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="prey">Prey</h3>
<p>Large diatom anomalies were above average during 2023–2025 <span class="citation" data-cites="ostlebatten2026diatoms">(<a href="#ref-ostlebatten2026diatoms" role="doc-biblioref">Ostle and Batten 2026</a>)</span>, and spring 2026 chlorophyll-a concentrations were average to high across the NBS and SEBS <span class="citation" data-cites="gannetal2026chlorophyll">(<a href="#ref-gannetal2026chlorophyll" role="doc-biblioref">Gann et al. 2026</a>)</span>. These records suggest favorable prey-production conditions in their respective periods. Increased surface phosphate and a deeper mixed layer in 2024 imply wind mixing, larger phytoplankton cells, shorter food chains and more efficient energy transfer to juvenile fish <span class="citation" data-cites="gann2026nutrients">(<a href="#ref-gann2026nutrients" role="doc-biblioref">Gann 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>The spring Rapid Zooplankton Assessment indicated adequate small copepod abundance, with <strong>above-average large copepod abundance by late summer</strong> <span class="citation" data-cites="kimmel2026zooplankton">(<a href="#ref-kimmel2026zooplankton" role="doc-biblioref">Kimmel et al. 2026</a>)</span>. Euphausiid abundance increased from 2025 <span class="citation" data-cites="levine2026euphausiids spear2026euphausiids">(<a href="#ref-levine2026euphausiids" role="doc-biblioref">Levine et al. 2026</a>; <a href="#ref-spear2026euphausiids" role="doc-biblioref">Spear et al. 2026</a>)</span>. Copepod and euphausiid lipid content in the SEBS were both above average in 2026, indicating good prey quality for pelagic juveniles <span class="citation" data-cites="pinger2026lipids">(<a href="#ref-pinger2026lipids" role="doc-biblioref">Pinger et al. 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Spring larval abundance and egg numbers were low, as was the larval condition ratio. Such observations are typical of cold spring conditions over the shelf, and temperature-dependent seasonal timing complicates their interpretation <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>. SEBS age-0 abundance was low <span class="citation" data-cites="andrews2026juvenileforage">(<a href="#ref-andrews2026juvenileforage" role="doc-biblioref">Andrews, Domke, Murphy, Spear, et al. 2026</a>)</span>, and age-0 energy density was above average <span class="citation" data-cites="page2026juvenileenergy">(<a href="#ref-page2026juvenileenergy" role="doc-biblioref">Page et al. 2026</a>)</span>. The suggested increase in age-1 abundance in this juvenile-survey comparison remains unverified. Length–weight residuals for small pollock (100–250 mm) in the EBS survey improved to just below the long-term mean <span class="citation" data-cites="prohaskarohan2026condition">(<a href="#ref-prohaskarohan2026condition" role="doc-biblioref">Prohaska and Rohan 2026</a>)</span>. In the NBS, age-0 abundance was average <span class="citation" data-cites="andrews2026juvenileforage">(<a href="#ref-andrews2026juvenileforage" role="doc-biblioref">Andrews, Domke, Murphy, Spear, et al. 2026</a>)</span> and energy density was below average <span class="citation" data-cites="page2026juvenileenergy">(<a href="#ref-page2026juvenileenergy" role="doc-biblioref">Page et al. 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="competitors">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="competitors">Competitors</h3>
<p>Pelagic forager biomass increased from 2025 to 2026 to above its long-term mean, largely driven by a 58% increase in pollock biomass <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026, 7–9</a>)</span>. Above-average zooplankton quantity and quality moderate concerns about competition for prey among young pollock. SEBS jellyfish biomass remained average <span class="citation" data-cites="buser2026jellyfish">(<a href="#ref-buser2026jellyfish" role="doc-biblioref">Buser 2026</a>)</span> to below average <span class="citation" data-cites="domke2026jellyfish">(<a href="#ref-domke2026jellyfish" role="doc-biblioref">Domke et al. 2026</a>)</span>. NBS jellyfish biomass continued its slow decline since 2023 and remained just above the time-series mean <span class="citation" data-cites="domke2026jellyfish">(<a href="#ref-domke2026jellyfish" role="doc-biblioref">Domke et al. 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Pacific herring and capelin biomass were below average in both the NBS and SEBS <span class="citation" data-cites="andrews2026herringcapelin">(<a href="#ref-andrews2026herringcapelin" role="doc-biblioref">Andrews, Domke, Murphy, Dimond, et al. 2026</a>)</span>. Bristol Bay sockeye salmon continued to decline from peak 2021/2022 levels <span class="citation" data-cites="cunningham2026sockeye">(<a href="#ref-cunningham2026sockeye" role="doc-biblioref">Cunningham et al. 2026</a>)</span>. Strong 2020 and 2022 sablefish year classes contributed to a growing, aging population that could compete for pelagic juvenile prey; direct evidence for that competition remains unavailable <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="predators">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="predators">Predators</h3>
<p>Adult pollock diets consisted primarily of copepods and euphausiids, with a low overall proportion of cannibalism in 2026 <span class="citation" data-cites="aydin2026diets">(<a href="#ref-aydin2026diets" role="doc-biblioref">Aydin 2026</a>)</span>. CNRG estimates show that age-1 predation mortality declined from 2025, while mortality due to cannibalism remained slightly above its long-term mean. The biomass of pollock consumed by conspecifics was approximately average and lower than in 2024 and 2025 <span class="citation" data-cites="holsmanaydin2026cannibalism">(<a href="#ref-holsmanaydin2026cannibalism" role="doc-biblioref">Holsman et al. 2026</a>)</span>. Adult Bristol Bay sockeye salmon, which prey on juvenile pollock, decreased from 2025 <span class="citation" data-cites="cunningham2026sockeye">(<a href="#ref-cunningham2026sockeye" role="doc-biblioref">Cunningham et al. 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Northern fur seal pup weights at St. Paul Island exceeded the average by more than one standard deviation, and maternal trip durations were the shortest in the time series. These indicators suggest high foraging success near the island. Age-0 pollock and herring had the highest frequency of occurrence in the September 2025 fur-seal diet samples; analysis of September 2026 samples was ongoing in the draft <span class="citation" data-cites="mchuron2026furseals">(<a href="#ref-mchuron2026furseals" role="doc-biblioref"><span class="nocase">McHuron et al.</span> 2026</a>)</span>. The apex predator guild increased from 2025, driven by a 17% increase in Pacific cod, and remained below its long-term mean <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026, 7–9</a>)</span>. This guild level suggests low predation pressure on juvenile pollock <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level2" data-number="11.2" id="sec-ecosystem-juveniles-adults">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-ecosystem-juveniles-adults" data-number="11.2"><span class="header-section-number">11.2</span> Ecosystem considerations for later juveniles and adults</h2>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="distribution">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="distribution">Distribution</h3>
<p>Pollock biomass estimated by the standard bottom-trawl survey increased approximately 50% from 2025 to 2026, alongside a pronounced spatial pattern associated with the extensive cold pool. Adult pollock occurred primarily outside bottom waters colder than 2°C, with concentrations along the northwestern outer shelf <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>. The cold pool therefore delineated the near-bottom habitat occupied by much of the adult population during the survey. This pattern is relevant to interpreting the biomass increase because survey catches reflect both the number and size of fish present and their availability to bottom-trawl gear. The higher survey estimate and the concentration of adults along the cold-pool margin should be considered together when comparing years. The spatial association supports a role for temperature in shaping survey availability, while the contribution of redistribution to the biomass increase remains unresolved.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="environmental-processes-1">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="environmental-processes-1">Environmental Processes</h3>
<p>Bottom temperatures in 2026 were comparable to the historical cool years 1986, 1992, 2006 and 2010 <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>. The large cold pool provided further evidence of cool bottom conditions <span class="citation" data-cites="rohanbarnett2026coldpool">(<a href="#ref-rohanbarnett2026coldpool" role="doc-biblioref">Rohan and Barnett 2026</a>)</span>. <strong>Below-average SSTs</strong> characterized the SEBS, particularly during spring <span class="citation" data-cites="lemagiecallahan2026sst">(<a href="#ref-lemagiecallahan2026sst" role="doc-biblioref">Lemagie and Callahan 2026</a>)</span>. Adult pollock condition was above its long-term mean <span class="citation" data-cites="prohaskarohan2026condition">(<a href="#ref-prohaskarohan2026condition" role="doc-biblioref">Prohaska and Rohan 2026</a>)</span>. These temperature and condition patterns describe concurrent conditions; their causal relationship remains an interpretation.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="prey-1">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="prey-1">Prey</h3>
<p>Adult pollock diets continued to be dominated by <strong>copepods</strong> and euphausiids <span class="citation" data-cites="aydin2026diets">(<a href="#ref-aydin2026diets" role="doc-biblioref">Aydin 2026</a>)</span>. Summer and late-summer euphausiid abundance increased from 2025 to 2026 <span class="citation" data-cites="levine2026euphausiids spear2026euphausiids">(<a href="#ref-levine2026euphausiids" role="doc-biblioref">Levine et al. 2026</a>; <a href="#ref-spear2026euphausiids" role="doc-biblioref">Spear et al. 2026</a>)</span>, and above-average SEBS copepod and euphausiid lipid content provided lipid-rich prey <span class="citation" data-cites="pinger2026lipids">(<a href="#ref-pinger2026lipids" role="doc-biblioref">Pinger et al. 2026</a>)</span>. Cannibalism formed a low proportion of adult pollock diets <span class="citation" data-cites="aydin2026diets">(<a href="#ref-aydin2026diets" role="doc-biblioref">Aydin 2026</a>)</span>. CNRG estimates separately indicate slightly above-average mortality of age-1 pollock from cannibalism, with approximately average biomass consumed by conspecifics <span class="citation" data-cites="holsmanaydin2026cannibalism">(<a href="#ref-holsmanaydin2026cannibalism" role="doc-biblioref">Holsman et al. 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Morphometric condition, measured as length–weight residuals, for large adult pollock (&gt;250 mm) in the EBS survey increased from 2023 to 2026 to above the long-term mean. The NBS condition series extends through 2025, when large-pollock condition remained positive and continued the increasing trend observed since 2021 <span class="citation" data-cites="prohaskarohan2026condition">(<a href="#ref-prohaskarohan2026condition" role="doc-biblioref">Prohaska and Rohan 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="competitors-1">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="competitors-1">Competitors</h3>
<p>The increase in pelagic forager biomass from 2025 to 2026 was primarily driven by pollock <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026, 7–9</a>)</span>, suggesting a potential increase in competition within the pollock population. Above-average prey quantity, prey quality and pollock length–weight residuals indicate adequate food resources. Increasing sablefish abundance represents potential competition for pelagic prey, with direct evidence still pending <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="predators-1">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="predators-1">Predators</h3>
<p>The apex predator guild, driven by Pacific cod, increased from 2025 and remained below its long-term mean <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026, 7–9</a>)</span>. This pattern suggests low predation pressure on pollock <span class="citation" data-cites="siddon2026ebs">(<a href="#ref-siddon2026ebs" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon 2026</a>)</span>. These associations provide context for the stock; independent evidence is needed to establish the underlying mechanisms. The Plan Team requested further examination of ecosystem contributions to retrospective behavior alongside the direct data-influence tests.</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level1" data-number="12" id="data-gaps-and-research-priorities">
<h1 data-number="12"><span class="header-section-number">12</span> Data gaps and research priorities</h1>
<p>The 2026 assessment compares the separately fitted configurations and the Model 26.1.2 marginal-estimation sensitivity using their matching observations and conditional observation diagnostics. Model 26.0 posterior uncertainty, predictive observation checks and nine retrospective fits are complete. The Model 26.1.2 retrospective diagnostic uses fixed full-model process SDs and a conditional full 2026 reference. The two Model 26.0 simulation-retrospective experiments compare conditional biomass and recruitment revisions with the observed-data results (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-model260-selftest">Section 6.3.1</a>). Each experiment uses ten simulated datasets to examine biomass and recruitment revisions.</p>
<p>Additional age-1 BTS selectivity and BTS data-influence tests are outside the scope of this assessment (PT-02 and PT-05). The comparisons describe differences in retrospective patterns. The weight-at-age comparison in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#sec-fishery-weights">Section 4.1.3</a> retains the distinction between estimated schedules and uncertainty carried into population and projection outputs.</p>
<p>A high research priority is to refine the statistical treatment of length compositions and age observations from the fishery, bottom-trawl survey (BTS), and acoustic-trawl survey (ATS), together with paired Fourier-transform near-infrared spectroscopy (FT-NIR) and traditional morphological ageing (TMA) observations. A more statistically rigorous framework should account for sampling structure, ageing error, uncertainty in conversions between ageing methods, and dependence among observations derived from the same samples. This work should guide composition weighting and the integration of length and age information, with the resulting methods and uncertainty treatment carried into future model specifications.</p>
<p>The treatment of early fishery data should also be refined relative to more recent observations. Research should evaluate changes in sampling coverage, age and length information, and fishing practices across periods, and use those differences to inform selectivity assumptions and observation weights. Comparisons should assess how alternative treatments affect recruitment, biomass trends, and retrospective behavior.</p>
<p>Further development of random-effects models should address temporal variation in selectivity and other population or observation processes. Priorities include identifying which sources of variability the data can resolve, evaluating correlation across ages and years, and estimating process variation within a coherent framework. Simulation tests, retrospective analyses, and predictive checks should evaluate model performance and the propagation of uncertainty into stock status and catch projections.</p>
<p>The Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) provides a basis for fuller implementation and use of dynamic structural equation models (DSEM). This work should develop and test hypothesized links among environmental conditions, prey, pollock condition, and recruitment, while accounting for observation uncertainty, missing years, and time lags. Evaluation should establish the stability and predictive value of these relationships and how ESP results can inform assessment interpretation, recruitment scenarios, and future model specifications.</p>
<p>Additional research questions include AVO uncertainty, the 2018 recruitment profile, and stock boundaries and connectivity.</p>
</section>

We also thank the AFSC age-and-growth staff for their continued excellence in promptly processing these samples.</p>

</section>

<tr class="gt_heading header">
<td class="gt_heading gt_title gt_font_normal gt_bottom_border" colspan="4">Historical pollock management and monitoring measures</td>
</tr>
<tr class="gt_col_headings even">
<th class="gt_col_heading gt_columns_bottom_border gt_left" data-quarto-table-cell-role="th" id="measure_period" scope="col">Year</th>

<tbody class="gt_table_body">
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1977</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Preliminary BSAI fishery management plan (FMP), including closure areas.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a>; <a href="table2-sources/historical-management-1997.pdf">History 1997</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1982</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">BSAI groundfish FMP implemented; Chinook salmon bycatch limits established for foreign trawlers.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a>; <a href="table2-sources/historical-management-1997.pdf">History 1997</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1984</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">BSAI groundfish optimum yield capped at 2 million t; Chinook salmon bycatch limits for foreign trawling reduced.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a>; <a href="table2-sources/historical-management-1997.pdf">History 1997</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1990</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Domestic observer program and associated data reporting began.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a>; <a href="table2-sources/observer-program-history.html">NOAA history</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1992</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Pollock allocations under the Western Alaska Community Development Quota (CDQ) program began.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1993–1994</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Donation program</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Prohibited Species Donation Program established in 1993; voluntary salmon donations in 1994 are reported in the accepted assessment history.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/salmon-bycatch-overview.html">Council overview</a>; <a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1994</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Council recommendation</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Council recommended minimum codend mesh/design standards; an implemented NMFS mesh rule is not established by the reviewed sources.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/historical-management-1997.pdf">History 1997</a>; <a href="table2-sources/gear-definition-analysis-2025.pdf#page=20">Gear review</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1994</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Reporting</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">NMFS began publishing individual-vessel bycatch rates online.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a>; <a href="table2-sources/historical-management-1997.pdf">History 1997</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1994–1995</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Emergency Chum Salmon Savings Area in 1994; permanent chum savings-area provisions under Amendment 35 in 1995, alongside the historical Chinook closure/trigger regime.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/salmon-management-review-2023.pdf#page=2">2023 notice history</a>; <a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1998</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Amendment 49 improved retention/utilization requirements for pollock and Pacific cod took effect January 3.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/utilization-retention-final-1997.html">Amendment 49</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1998</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Enacted</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">American Fisheries Act (AFA) enacted, establishing the framework for sector allocations and fishery cooperatives.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a>; <a href="table2-sources/AFA-final-2000.html">AFA rule</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1999</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">AFA provisions implemented for catcher/processors.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a>; <a href="table2-sources/AFA-final-2000.html">AFA rule</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">1999</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Emergency rule</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Temporal/spatial pollock dispersal measures and trawl exclusion zones around selected Steller sea lion rookeries and haulouts in BSAI and GOA.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/sea-lion-emergency-1999.html">1999 emergency rule</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2000</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">AFA provisions implemented for the remaining catcher-vessel and mothership sectors.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a>; <a href="table2-sources/AFA-final-2000.html">AFA rule</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2001</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Voluntary</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Pollock industry began the chum salmon rolling-hotspot program.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/salmon-management-review-2023.pdf#page=2">2023 notice history</a>; <a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2002</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Voluntary</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Pollock industry began the Chinook salmon rolling-hotspot program.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/salmon-management-review-2023.pdf#page=2">2023 notice history</a>; <a href="table2-sources/assessment2024-official.pdf#page=63">SAFE 2024</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2005</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Council action</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Council selected Amendment 84 in October to provide a salmon bycatch intercooperative agreement (ICA) alternative to fixed savings-area closures.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/amendment84-final-2007.pdf">Amendment 84</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2006</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Exempted fishing</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">The B-season exempted fishing permit tested the ICA/rolling-hotspot approach before general regulatory implementation.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/amendment84-final-2007.pdf">Amendment 84</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2007</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Amendment 84 regulations, effective November 28, exempted pollock vessels participating in an approved salmon bycatch ICA from specified savings-area closures.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/amendment84-final-2007.pdf">Amendment 84</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2010–2011</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Rule / program</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Amendment 91 final rule effective September 29, 2010; Chinook PSC limits, incentive plan agreements (IPAs), performance standards and enhanced monitoring operated in the 2011 fishery.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/amendment91-final-2010.pdf">Amendment 91</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2015</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Council action</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Council took final action on Amendment 110 in April, recommending linked Chinook/chum avoidance measures and abundance-based Chinook limits.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/amendment110-final-2016.pdf">Amendment 110</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2016</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">Implemented</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">Amendment 110 final rule published June 10, effective July 11. It strengthened IPAs and changed pollock seasonal allocations to 45% A season / 55% B season.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/amendment110-final-2016.pdf">Amendment 110</a></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_period">2017</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_stage">First index year</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_description">First fishing year informed by the Amendment 110 three-system abundance index in 2016. Low-abundance limits apply when the index is at or below 250,000 Chinook salmon.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="measure_sources"><a href="table2-sources/amendment110-final-2016.pdf">Amendment 110</a></td>
</tr>
</tbody><tfoot>
<tr class="gt_sourcenotes odd">
<td class="gt_sourcenote" colspan="4">Historical entries were checked against accepted 2024 SAFE Table 4 (p. 63) and the linked primary sources. The 1994 codend item is a Council recommendation; the reviewed sources do not establish NMFS implementation. The 2005 Amendment 84 action preceded exempted fishing and 2007 regulations. Council action and rule effective dates are distinct.</td>
</tr>
<tr class="gt_sourcenotes even">
<td class="gt_sourcenote" colspan="4">The 45% / 55% allocation in the 2016 rule concerns pollock, distinct from Chinook PSC apportionments. Continuing and dated 2026 measures are described in Fishery and management history. Age-estimation and survey developments are documented in their respective report sections; they are not listed here as regulatory implementations.</td>
</tr>
<tr class="gt_sourcenotes odd">
<td class="gt_sourcenote" colspan="4"><a href="table2-sources/ebs_pollock_management_measures.csv">CSV</a>; <a href="table2-sources/ebs_pollock_management_measures.md">Markdown</a>; <a href="table2-sources/row-review.json">row-by-row verification and corrections</a>. Original source records remain unchanged.</td>
</tr>
</tfoot>
</table>

<span class="safe-caption-label">Table 3:</span> <span class="safe-caption-text">EBS pollock catch by reporting area and season, 1991–2026 (tons). Southeast (SE) comprises NMFS areas 520–539; Northwest (NW) comprises areas 500–517 and 519. Area 518 (Bogoslof) is excluded. A and B group records with week-ending dates before June 1 and from June 1 onward, respectively. The catch data extend through October 17, 2026. Only the 1998 records included catch without an area; this catch is allocated between NW and SE in proportion to reported catch within each season. Totals include retained and discarded catch; values are rounded to whole tons.
</span></figcaption>

<span class="safe-caption-label">Table 4:</span> <span class="safe-caption-text">Retained and discarded EBS pollock catch by reporting area, 1991–2026 (tons), from annual catch-accounting data. Values are rounded to whole tons; 2026 estimates are preliminary.

<span class="safe-caption-label">Table 5:</span> <span class="safe-caption-text">EBS pollock fishery catch-at-age estimates, 1964–2025 (million fish). Ages 15 and older are pooled as 15+. Catch numbers are calculated from assessment proportions, annual fishery weights at age and catch biomass where complete annual numbers are unavailable. Age-specific values are rounded to 0.1 million fish; All ages totals are rounded to the nearest million fish.
</span></figcaption>

</div><p><small>Source: AKFIN / NMFS Alaska Regional Office FMP catch export. Estimates sum retained and discarded catch across both pollock target categories and all reported gears in the BS subarea. Pollock, salmon, halibut, Non TAC Species, and records without a species group are excluded. Other combines remaining named source groups, including other flatfish and rockfish, Greenland turbot, Alaska plaice, squid, octopus, sculpins, and historical Other / Other Species groups; definitions follow the source export rather than a fixed modern FMP list. NA means no records for that category and year, rather than a measured zero. Source group names and the complete column map are available with the annual CSV. Values are summed before rounding; units are metric tons. The 2026 estimates are preliminary through the week ending October 24. <a href="tables/fmp-species-in-pollock.csv">Download annual estimates (CSV)</a> · <a href="tables/fmp-species-column-map.csv">Column definitions (CSV)</a>.</small></p></section>

</div><p><small>Source: AKFIN / NMFS Alaska Regional Office FMP catch export, BS subarea. Estimates include retained and discarded pollock catch and all reported gears. Pollock-directed trips, blank trip targets, and No retained catch targets are excluded. Other.flats combines flathead sole, arrowtooth flounder, other flatfish, Alaska plaice, Kamchatka flounder, and Greenland turbot targets. Other.spp combines the remaining identified targets: rockfish, sablefish, Atka mackerel, Other Species, and halibut. Rock.sole is the source Rock Sole - BSAI target; it is not restricted to a separately identified northern rock sole target. NA means no records for that target group and year. Total sums the included unrounded values; displayed columns may differ from Total by rounding. Units are metric tons. The 2026 estimates are preliminary through the week ending October 31. The complete target map and exclusion totals accompany the annual CSV. <a href="tables/pollock-in-other-fisheries.csv">Download annual estimates (CSV)</a> · <a href="tables/pollock-bycatch-target-map.csv">Column definitions (CSV)</a>.</small></p></section>

</div><p><small>Source: AKFIN / NMFS Alaska Regional Office nontarget catch-accounting export. BSAI records (BS and AI) are included; GOA and inside-water records are excluded. Both pollock target categories, all reported gears, and retained and discarded records are combined using Nontarget Estimate (mt), not the species-count field. Squid, sculpins, and seabirds are outside the selected groups of this table and are excluded. MiscFish is the source Misc fish group. Osmerid combines capelin, eulachon, other osmerids, family Osmeridae smelts, and surf smelt; Grenadier combines all named grenadier groups. Other contains the remaining selected fish and invertebrate groups; the complete mapping accompanies the annual CSV. NA means no records for a group-year; a displayed zero may be a positive estimate below 0.5 t. Values are summed before rounding to whole metric tons. The 2026 estimates are preliminary through the week ending October 24. The November 2024 summary approximately doubled the 2019-2022 Jellies, MiscFish, SeaStar, Osmerid, Grenadier, and Eelpouts columns relative to September. Sea pen, Anemone, Snails, and Other changed non-uniformly, with cross-column numerical matches indicating changed alignment or allocation. These are comparisons of historical headers. The current table uses explicit source species names and both catch dispositions, with no scaling adjustment. The upstream preparation step remains unconfirmed. <a href="validation/jellyfish-audit.html">View the jellyfish source-history and filter audit</a>. <a href="tables/nontarget-species-bycatch.csv">Download annual estimates (CSV)</a> · <a href="tables/nontarget-species-column-map.csv">Column definitions (CSV)</a>.</small></p></section><div class="cell">

<div class="cell quarto-float quarto-figure quarto-figure-center anchored" id="tbl-ats-biomass">
<figure class="quarto-float quarto-float-tbl figure">
<figcaption class="quarto-float-caption-top quarto-float-caption quarto-float-tbl safe-caption safe-caption-hanging safe-caption-hanging" data-safe-caption-layout="label-hanging-text" id="tbl-ats-biomass-caption-0ceaefa1-69ba-4598-a22c-09a6ac19f8ca">
<span class="safe-caption-label">Table 18:</span> <span class="safe-caption-text">Midwater pollock biomass by area from summer ATS surveys of the U.S. EEZ Bering Sea shelf, 1994–2026 (million tons; near surface to 0.5 m above the seafloor). The core shelf excludes the Northern Extension. Assessment CVs average 20%, with 45% assigned to 2000; SE equals biomass × CV. The 2020 survey used uncrewed sailing vessels; 2026 estimates are preliminary.
</span></figcaption>
<div aria-describedby="tbl-ats-biomass-caption-0ceaefa1-69ba-4598-a22c-09a6ac19f8ca">

Mean and median summarize surveys with age compositions during 1994–2026; 1979–1991 provides historical context.

<span class="safe-caption-label">Table 36:</span> <span class="safe-caption-text">Model 26.0 biological schedules and fishery weight predictions at ages 1–15+, with weights for 2024–2026. <span class="safe-caption-label">Table 43:</span> <span class="safe-caption-text">Model 26.0 retrospective terminal estimates and revisions: All rows use the full-2026 reference. Each row omits all observations after its terminal year, using the same data-lag rules. Relative revisions are 100 × (peel estimate / full-2026-fit estimate for the same calendar year − 1). SSB is female spawning biomass; F is the maximum age-specific fishing mortality. These are point-estimate comparisons; the peel comparisons cover population estimates only.

<span class="safe-caption-label">Figure 3:</span> <span class="safe-caption-text">Cumulative EBS pollock catch as a proportion of annual specified TAC for weeks ending in January, February, March, and April, 2000–2026. <a class="lightbox" data-gallery="quarto-lightbox-gallery-49" href="assets/figure-050.png" title="Figure 50: ATS-q negative log marginal density and likelihood profile for Model 26.0. Panel A compares the negative log of the MCMC marginal density, normalized to integrate to one, with the optimized profile NLL. Each curve is measured relative to its own minimum over ATS q. The marginal density uses a kernel estimate from all 5,000 saved draws. Panel B pairs weighted quadratic regressions fitted directly to all 5,000 MCMC component values with profile NLL contributions for composition data, index data and selectivity deviates. The smoothers use individual draws and are displayed over the central 99% of sampled ATS q. MCMC curves are centered at the ATS-q marginal mode; profile components retain the profile minimum as their reference. These smoothers describe conditional mean native objective components; the negative log marginal density has no unique additive decomposition into those components. Other is omitted."><img alt="Panel A shows the negative log normalized ATS-q marginal density and profile NLL, each centered at its minimum. Panel B compares dashed quadratic MCMC component curves with solid profile component curves for three terms." aria-label="Panel A shows the negative log normalized ATS-q marginal density and profile NLL, each centered at its minimum. <span class="safe-caption-label">Figure 50:</span> <span class="safe-caption-text">ATS-q negative log marginal density and likelihood profile for Model 26.0. Panel A compares the negative log of the MCMC marginal density, normalized to integrate to one, with the optimized profile NLL. Each curve is measured relative to its own minimum over ATS q. The marginal density uses a kernel estimate from all 5,000 saved draws. Panel B pairs weighted quadratic regressions fitted directly to all 5,000 MCMC component values with profile NLL contributions for composition data, index data and selectivity deviates. The smoothers use individual draws and are displayed over the central 99% of sampled ATS q. MCMC curves are centered at the ATS-q marginal mode; profile components retain the profile minimum as their reference. These smoothers describe conditional mean native objective components; the negative log marginal density has no unique additive decomposition into those components. Other is omitted.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</div>

<table class="gt_table cell caption-top table table-sm table-striped small" data-quarto-bootstrap="false">
<thead>
<tr class="gt_heading header">
<td class="gt_heading gt_title gt_font_normal gt_bottom_border" colspan="4">SSC and Plan Team requests</td>
</tr>
<tr class="gt_col_headings even">
<th class="gt_col_heading gt_columns_bottom_border gt_left" data-quarto-table-cell-role="th" id="ID" scope="col">ID</th>
<th class="gt_col_heading gt_columns_bottom_border gt_left" data-quarto-table-cell-role="th" id="Recommendation" scope="col">Recommendation</th>
<th class="gt_col_heading gt_columns_bottom_border gt_left" data-quarto-table-cell-role="th" id="Response" scope="col">Response</th>
<th class="gt_col_heading gt_columns_bottom_border gt_left" data-quarto-table-cell-role="th" id="Response-status" scope="col">Response status</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="gt_table_body">
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="ID">PT-01</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Recommendation">Bring Model 26.0 forward for management use in November and present Model 23.0 for continuity and comparison during the transition to Rceattle.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Response">Model 26.0 estimates, uncertainty, diagnostics, Tier 3 projections and Model 23.0 comparisons are presented. Regularized posterior summaries, predictive checks and observed and simulated-data retrospectives are included. Model 26.1.2 is a sensitivity comparison conditional on fixed Foreign and Modern process SDs of 0.1235 and 0.582. Risk categories are Level 1.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Response status">Assessment results and sensitivity comparisons presented</td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="ID">PT-02</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Recommendation">Evaluate alternative treatments of age-1 BTS selectivity, including the selectivity penalty and a time-invariant alternative, to assess their influence on the retrospective pattern.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Response">The author proposes no additional age-1 BTS selectivity sensitivities for this assessment. Observed and simulated-data retrospective results are presented; these results do not separately identify the effect of an alternative age-1 selectivity treatment.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Response status">No additional age-1 selectivity tests proposed</td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="ID">PT-03</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Recommendation">Extend the Model 26.0 self-test with retrospective peels on simulated datasets generated from the fitted model, and examine retrospective patterns in time-varying selectivity estimates.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Response">Two sets of ten simulated datasets use the fitted parameters and ten regularized posterior draws, respectively. Each dataset has a full-2026 fit and nine peels ending in 2017–2025. Observed spawning-biomass rho (+0.121) exceeds every simulated value in both sets. Posterior diagnostics and predictive checks are also presented. The simulations assess population revisions; they establish no single retrospective cause.</td>
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="Response status">Paired simulation retrospectives and posterior predictive checks presented</td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td class="gt_row gt_left" headers="ID">PT-04</td>
