<section class="level2 unnumbered safe-appendix-heading" id="sec-esp-2026-appendix">
<h2 class="unnumbered safe-appendix-heading anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-esp-2026-appendix"><span class="safe-appendix-label"><strong>Appendix B</strong></span><br/>
<span class="safe-appendix-title"><strong>Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile of Eastern Bering Sea Walleye Pollock</strong></span></h2>
<p>This draft Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) for EBS pollock brings together substantial work completed to date and provides a starting point for future ESP Team discussions. An AI agent helped compile and coordinate material from disparate information sources and research activities. Over the next year, the EBS pollock ESP Team will formalize its membership and begin meetings that engage a broader group of scientific experts to develop the profile. Please contact Jim Ianelli and Kalei Shotwell with questions or for further details about this document or the EBS pollock ESP.</p>
<div aria-label="Draft EBS pollock Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile" class="esp2026-draft" role="region">
<div aria-label="ESP authors and logo" class="esp2026-cover"><img alt="Pollock ESP hexagonal emblem with a fish silhouette and ecosystem, socioeconomic, and research imagery." aria-label="Pollock ESP hexagonal emblem with a fish silhouette and ecosystem, socioeconomic, and research imagery." class="esp2026-logo" role="img" src="assets/pollock-esp-hex-sticker.png"/></div>
<nav aria-label="ESP appendix contents" id="esp2026-contents"><p><strong>Contents</strong></p><ol><li><a href="#esp2026-executive-summary">Executive Summary</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-responses-to-ssc-and-plan-team-comments-on-esps-in-general">Responses to SSC and Plan Team Comments on ESPs in General</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-responses-to-ssc-and-plan-team-comments-specific-to-ebs-pollock">Responses to SSC and Plan Team Comments Specific to EBS Pollock</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-introduction">Introduction</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-indicator-synthesis">Indicator Synthesis</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-indicator-assessment">Indicator Assessment</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-data-gaps-and-future-research-priorities">Data Gaps and Future Research Priorities</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-conclusion">Conclusion</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-literature-cited">Literature Cited</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-tables">Tables</a></li><li><a href="#esp2026-figures">Figures</a></li></ol></nav>
<section class="level3" id="esp2026-executive-summary">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-executive-summary">Executive Summary</h3>
<p>The Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) connects stock-specific environmental, biological, fishery, and community information with assessment interpretation and management questions. Its sequence of focus, synthesis, analysis, and communication provides a structured way to evaluate proposed indicators <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-shotwell2023esp">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-shotwell2023esp" role="doc-biblioref">Shotwell et al. 2023</a>)</span>. This draft focuses initially on recruitment to age 1, then identifies processes affecting juvenile survival to age 3, adult growth and condition, survey interpretation, and fishery performance.</p>
<p>The ESP distinguishes two DSEM applications. The archived Rceattle pilot evaluates birth-year SST and age-1-year cold-pool proxies <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-ianelli2026developments">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-ianelli2026developments" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2026</a>)</span>. A separate age-1 DSEM working paper analyzes 18 ecosystem series alongside an age-1 response estimated by the assessment.  Regional age-0 energy density provides an additional measured-condition series <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-page2026energy">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-page2026energy" role="doc-biblioref">Page and Maselko 2026</a>)</span>. </p>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-acceptable-biological-catch-considerations">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-acceptable-biological-catch-considerations">Acceptable Biological Catch Considerations</h4>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-candidate-predictive-indicators">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-candidate-predictive-indicators">Candidate Predictive Indicators</h5>
<p>Fall age-0 total energy, prey quality and abundance, and juvenile–predator overlap are priorities for testing. Field studies connect fall total energy with age-1 recruits per spawner, and laboratory experiments identify body size and energy reserves as determinants of survival during food deprivation <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-heintz2013 esp2026-sogard2000">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-heintz2013" role="doc-biblioref">Heintz et al. 2013</a>; <a href="#ref-esp2026-sogard2000" role="doc-biblioref">Sogard and Olla 2000</a>)</span>. Studies of pollock recruitment and spatial predation identify juvenile overlap with adult pollock and arrowtooth flounder as another important pathway <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-mueter2006 esp2026-spencer2016">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-mueter2006" role="doc-biblioref">Mueter et al. 2006</a>; <a href="#ref-esp2026-spencer2016" role="doc-biblioref">Spencer et al. 2016</a>)</span>. </p>
<p>The regional energy-density series contain 21 southeastern Bering Sea (SEBS) and 15 northern Bering Sea (NBS) annual means within 2002–2025, measured in kJ/g dry mass. The latest values, for 2025, are 19.23 and 20.84 kJ/g dry mass for SEBS and NBS, respectively. Both are lower than their 2024 observations; a 2026 energy-density observation is absent. Sampling metadata, observation uncertainty, and forecast evaluation remain prerequisites for a predictive role <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-page2026energy">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-page2026energy" role="doc-biblioref">Page and Maselko 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-contextual-indicators">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-contextual-indicators">Contextual Indicators</h5>
<p>Sea ice, seasonal temperature, cold-pool extent, plankton and euphausiids, age-0 abundance and condition, adult condition, weight-at-age, and predator overlap form the initial contextual set. The relevant biological question is whether each cohort encounters adequate prey, accumulates energy before winter, and survives subsequent predation. The poor 2007 cohort illustrates why a favorable temperature category alone can give an incomplete account: low summer production and poor age-0 condition occurred during a cold year <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-gann2016">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-gann2016" role="doc-biblioref">Gann et al. 2016</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>The 2026 physical and prey indicators show a mixed pattern relative to their own observed-period means. Sea ice and cold-pool extent are above those means; SST and bottom temperature are below. The open-water bloom indicator is lower, while chlorophyll a is higher. Spring small and large copepods and summer small copepods are below their respective means; summer large copepods are slightly above. <a href="#esp2026-recorded-annual-indicators"></a></p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-fishery-informed-indicators">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-fishery-informed-indicators">Fishery Informed Indicators</h5>
<p>Candidate indicators include age and size composition of catch, fishery weight-at-age, season and area of harvest, standardized fishery catch rates, catch and quota utilization, and salmon bycatch measures. Their interpretation must account for fishing choices, allocation and avoidance behavior, processing demand, and reporting coverage. These indicators may reveal operational changes or sampling differences that help interpret assessment inputs. Their proposed inclusion in this ESP requires a defined management question.</p>
<p>The draft supports evaluation of ecosystem and fishery concerns in the SAFE risk table. Any resulting change in risk classification or ABC must be documented by the assessment authors using the completed annual synthesis and assessment results. ABC and OFL remain unchanged by this contribution.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-total-allowable-catch-considerations">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-total-allowable-catch-considerations">Total Allowable Catch Considerations</h4>
<p>Verified economic context covers BSAI catch, participation, ex-vessel and first-wholesale statistics through 2024, and U.S.-national trade through 2025 (<a href="#esp2026-economic-observations">Catch and Market Context</a>). These scopes differ from the BS assessment stock and from each other. A <strong>speculative 2026 interpretation</strong> is that firmer product unit values could support gross returns, while operating costs and product mix could offset those gains unevenly among vessels, processors and communities. 2026 margins and community outcomes remain uncertain. This interpretation is qualitative.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level3" id="esp2026-responses-to-ssc-and-plan-team-comments-on-esps-in-general">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-responses-to-ssc-and-plan-team-comments-on-esps-in-general">Responses to SSC and Plan Team Comments on ESPs in General</h3>
<p>A summary of potential SSC/PT comments on ESPs in general includes: distinguish predictive from contextual indicators, evaluate competing mechanistic explanations, document DSEM diagnostics, and coordinate economic and community information with existing Council products. This pollock contribution addresses those questions by defining indicator roles, documenting the fitted pilot and its diagnostic limitation, and proposing an explicit socioeconomic inventory. </p>
</section>
<section class="level3" id="esp2026-responses-to-ssc-and-plan-team-comments-specific-to-ebs-pollock">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-responses-to-ssc-and-plan-team-comments-specific-to-ebs-pollock">Responses to SSC and Plan Team Comments Specific to EBS Pollock</h3>
<p><strong>December 2024 SSC, EBS Ecosystem Status Report (page 3):</strong> the SSC recommended pollock-focused DSEM work to reconcile contrasting larval, juvenile-condition, and adult signals, and to investigate changed recruitment relationships <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-npfmc2024ssc">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-npfmc2024ssc" role="doc-biblioref">North Pacific Fishery Management Council Scientific and Statistical Committee 2024</a>)</span>. </p>
<p><strong>Contribution to that work:</strong> The starter age-1 DSEM analysis appears in the 2026 EBS Ecosystem Status Report (Siddon 2026).<span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-siddon2026coordination"><a href="#ref-esp2026-siddon2026coordination" role="doc-biblioref"></a></span></p>
<p>The assessment website records continuing work on contrasting early-life observations, cannibalism and biomass consumed, multispecies mortality, weight-at-age and condition, and stock distribution across U.S. and Russian waters <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-ianelli2026ssc">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-ianelli2026ssc" role="doc-biblioref">EBS Pollock Assessment Team 2026</a>)</span>. Its retained earlier responses carry an explicit requirement for verification before use as final results. This draft translates those topics into proposed ESP tasks.</p>
<p data-esp-format-addition="cross-reference">Pollock review topics and proposed ESP contributions are summarized in <a href="#esp2026-tbl-review">Table B1</a>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3" id="esp2026-introduction">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-introduction">Introduction</h3>
<p>Pollock recruitment reflects survival through several life stages with different food requirements, habitats, and predator exposure. Large differences in egg or larval abundance can be modified by later feeding, growth, transport, and mortality. The first-year review by Duffy-Anderson et al. provides the organizing synthesis for these processes <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-duffyanderson2016">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-duffyanderson2016" role="doc-biblioref">Duffy-Anderson et al. 2016</a>)</span>. The local recruitment review extends that structure through ages 1 and 2 to survival at age 3. In this appendix, <strong>age-1 recruitment</strong> is the focal response used by the DSEM pilot; <strong>survival to age 3</strong> is a separate later-stage outcome that retains the identity of the same birth cohort.</p>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-justification">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-justification">Justification</h4>
<p>The ESP creates an evidence trail from a biological or socioeconomic question to an indicator and its proposed use. For EBS pollock, the immediate question is whether early-life information can improve interpretation of uncertain recruitment and future biomass. Additional questions concern adult productivity, changing spatial availability to surveys, fishery operations, and community exposure. The September 2026 document provides the starting framework for developing this appendix <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-ianelli2026developments">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-ianelli2026developments" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-data">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-data">Data</h4>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-contributor--age-0-energy-density">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-contributor--age-0-energy-density">Age-0 Energy Density</h5>
<p>Annual mean energy density of age-0 walleye pollock is available for the northern and southeastern Bering Sea during 2002–2025, in <strong>kJ/g dry mass</strong> <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-page2026energy">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-page2026energy" role="doc-biblioref">Page and Maselko 2026</a>)</span>. Johanna Page (Vollenweider) provided the data, with Jacek Maselko as a co-contact. The southeastern series contains 21 annual means and the northern series contains 15. Both regions lack observations for 2003, 2013 and 2020; the northern series also lacks 2008–2012 and 2014. </p>
<p data-esp-format-addition="cross-reference">The source inventory and remaining data-assembly needs are summarized in <a href="#esp2026-tbl-data">Table B2</a>.</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level3" id="esp2026-indicator-synthesis">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-indicator-synthesis">Indicator Synthesis</h3>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-ecosystem-processes">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-ecosystem-processes">Ecosystem Processes</h4>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-spawning-supply-and-transport">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-spawning-supply-and-transport">Spawning Supply and Transport</h5>
<p>Spawning biomass and spawning location influence egg and early-larval supply. Smart et al. found associations between spawning biomass and early stages, with weaker correspondence after early larval development <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-smart2012">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-smart2012" role="doc-biblioref">Smart et al. 2012</a>)</span>. Transport and the spatial arrangement of spawning also matter. The biophysical model of Petrik et al. reproduced warm–cold distribution differences most successfully through changes in spawning areas <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-petrik2015">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-petrik2015" role="doc-biblioref">Petrik et al. 2015</a>)</span>. These results support separate hypotheses for cohort supply, transport, and access to nursery habitat.</p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-feeding-and-fall-age-0-condition">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-feeding-and-fall-age-0-condition">Feeding and Fall Age-0 Condition</h5>
<p>Prey availability includes amount, nutritional quality, and spatial match with fish. Larval copepod concentrations and frontal habitat illustrate why a broad regional biomass index can differ from prey encountered by an individual fish <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-smart2012 esp2026-brodeur2000">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-smart2012" role="doc-biblioref">Smart et al. 2012</a>; <a href="#ref-esp2026-brodeur2000" role="doc-biblioref">Brodeur et al. 2000</a>)</span>. Diet studies show that prey use varies with fish size and that pollock and Pacific cod can partition prey <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-buckley2016 esp2026-strasburger2014">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-buckley2016" role="doc-biblioref">Buckley et al. 2016</a>; <a href="#ref-esp2026-strasburger2014" role="doc-biblioref">Strasburger et al. 2014</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Siddon et al. describe a seasonal shift from larval growth and development toward lipid storage after transformation to the juvenile stage <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-siddon2013">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-siddon2013" role="doc-biblioref">Siddon et al. 2013</a>)</span>. Heintz et al. found higher diet lipid content and age-0 energy density during cold conditions in their study; fall total energy was positively associated with age-1 recruits per spawner <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-heintz2013">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-heintz2013" role="doc-biblioref">Heintz et al. 2013</a>)</span>. Moss et al. also documented differences in age-0 energetic condition and food habits across thermal conditions <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-moss2009">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-moss2009" role="doc-biblioref">Moss et al. 2009</a>)</span>. These findings motivate indicators of energy density, body mass, and total energy with explicit measurement definitions. The annual series measures energy density in kJ/g dry mass. </p>
<p>Eisner et al. evaluated large copepods as leading indicators of age-3 pollock abundance for the 2002–2015 year classes, excluding 2013 <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-eisner2020copepods">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-eisner2020copepods" role="doc-biblioref">Eisner et al. 2020</a>)</span>. Their comparison reinforces the value of prey information while identifying a specific cohort range and recruitment age. </p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-overwinter-survival">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-overwinter-survival">Overwinter Survival</h5>
<p>Fall condition provides the starting reserves for the first winter. Sogard and Olla’s food-deprivation experiments show that greater size, higher initial condition, and colder water can extend survival <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-sogard2000">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-sogard2000" role="doc-biblioref">Sogard and Olla 2000</a>)</span>. Field survival also involves winter feeding, movement, and predators. Laboratory results therefore support a mechanism and its direction, while annual field data are needed to quantify its effect on recruitment.</p>
<p>Sea ice, bloom timing, summer mixing, and temperature influence prey production and energy demand. Sigler et al. connect annual production of copepods, euphausiids, and juvenile pollock with seasonal environmental conditions <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-sigler2016">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-sigler2016" role="doc-biblioref">Sigler et al. 2016</a>)</span>. Gann et al.’s analysis of 2007 identifies a plausible production limitation during a cold year <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-gann2016">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-gann2016" role="doc-biblioref">Gann et al. 2016</a>)</span>. The ESP should evaluate these intermediate processes before interpreting a simple warm–cold contrast as a cohort forecast.</p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-predation-and-later-juvenile-survival">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-predation-and-later-juvenile-survival">Predation and Later Juvenile Survival</h5>
<p>Adult pollock can increase juvenile mortality through cannibalism, while arrowtooth flounder and other predators create additional exposure. Mueter et al. identify both food-related and predation-related controls on pollock recruitment, including juvenile–adult overlap <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-mueter2006">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-mueter2006" role="doc-biblioref">Mueter et al. 2006</a>)</span>. Spencer et al. model spatial predation by arrowtooth flounder and show how cold-pool extent can alter predator access to juvenile habitat <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-spencer2016">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-spencer2016" role="doc-biblioref">Spencer et al. 2016</a>)</span>. </p>
<p>The timing of predation matters for the response. A summer overlap or cold-pool observation in year <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+1</annotation></semantics></math> occurs after the beginning of the cohort’s age-1 year. Its use to explain an age-1 entry state requires explicit justification or a revised response definition. Such observations may be more directly aligned with survival during age 1 and later ages. </p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-adult-productivity-and-observation-processes">
<p data-esp-format-addition="cross-reference">Life stages, processes and priority observations are summarized in <a href="#esp2026-tbl-life-history">Table B3</a>.</p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-workshop-conceptual-models-for-recruitment-and-growth">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-workshop-conceptual-models-for-recruitment-and-growth">Workshop Conceptual Models for Recruitment and Growth</h5>
<p>The January 2025 pollock biology and ecology workshop developed preliminary conceptual models for Bering Sea recruitment and growth <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-monnahan2026workshop">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-monnahan2026workshop" role="doc-biblioref">Monnahan et al. 2026</a>)</span>. <a class="quarto-xref" href="#esp2026-fig-workshop-recruitment">Figure B1</a> organizes reproductive output, seasonal juvenile stages, prey quality, energetic condition, predation, and cold-pool extent. <a class="quarto-xref" href="#esp2026-fig-workshop-growth">Figure B2</a> connects population weight-at-age with somatic growth, size-selective mortality, prey, competitors, fishing, and physical conditions. Together they support an ESP that examines recruitment and growth. </p>
<p><strong>Recruitment pathways:</strong> spawning biomass and fecundity inform reproductive output. Seasonal surveys track the cohort from spring age 0 through age 2. Diet, krill, copepods, and prey lipid measurements inform forage quality and juvenile energetic condition; predation indices and cold-pool extent inform later survival. The diagram highlights both candidate observations and intermediate biological states.</p>
<p><strong>Growth pathways:</strong> the model separates growth of surviving fish from changes in population weight-at-age associated with size-selective mortality. Prey availability, density, genetic diversity, and spatial history enter the growth network alongside physical conditions and zooplankton. This distinction supports age- and season-specific weight and condition indicators with explicit survey or fishery sampling definitions.</p>
<p>The cohort sequence in <a class="quarto-xref" href="#esp2026-fig-pathways">Figure B3</a> summarizes the recruitment mechanisms developed in this draft and extends the survival question to age 3. The workshop diagrams provide a broader set of hypotheses for future indicator development.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-socioeconomic-processes">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-socioeconomic-processes">Socioeconomic Processes</h4>
<p>Biological supply, access to fishing grounds, operating costs, product demand, and processing capacity can jointly affect realized harvest and its value. Those processes may alter where and when vessels fish, the size and age of fish landed, and the distribution of benefits. This component should therefore connect each indicator to a concrete question, such as whether lower quota utilization reflects reduced fish availability, market conditions, processing limits, or avoidance behavior.</p>
<p>The Economic SAFE provides source categories for catch, discards, prohibited species catch, production and value, participation, and effort <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-noaa2026economic">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-noaa2026economic" role="doc-biblioref">Alaska Fisheries Science Center 2026b</a>)</span>. This draft proposes species- and sector-specific summaries where the source supports that detail. Community analysis requires clear distinctions among landing ports, vessel ownership, workforce residence, processor location, and CDQ beneficiaries. Each describes a different form of participation or exposure.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-proposed-indicators">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-proposed-indicators">Proposed Indicators</h4>
<p>The mechanism table (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#esp2026-tbl-mechanisms">Table B4</a>) links a driver, a measurable process, and the intended response. Expected directions are hypotheses for the stated pathway. Several upstream physical effects depend on season, prey response, and spatial coverage, so their net sign can change across conditions.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level3" id="esp2026-indicator-assessment">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-indicator-assessment">Indicator Assessment</h3>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-indicator-selection">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-indicator-selection">Indicator Selection</h4>
<p>Selection starts with a mechanistic explanation, the population or socioeconomic response, and the date when the information becomes available. Candidates then require reliable annual production, adequate spatial and temporal coverage, quantified uncertainty, and additional information beyond the other indicators.</p>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-ecosystem-indicators">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-ecosystem-indicators">Ecosystem Indicators</h5>
<p>The initial set should remain small enough for scientific review: seasonal physical forcing; a documented prey index; fall age-0 size and energetic condition; juvenile–predator overlap or a reviewed mortality product; and adult growth and condition. Larval supply and transport add value when annual coverage and biological alignment support them. Indicator families should be assessed together so correlated temperature, ice, and prey signals receive an interpretation that accounts for shared processes.</p>
</section>
<p>The available age-0 energy-density series describe regional energetic condition (<a href="#esp2026-fig-energy-density">Figure B4</a>). The histories of the ecosystem inputs and age-1 response provide context for the DSEM analysis (<a href="#esp2026-fig-working-indicators">Figure B5</a>).</p>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-socioeconomic-indicators">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-socioeconomic-indicators">Socioeconomic Indicators</h5>
<p data-esp-format-addition="cross-reference">Proposed socioeconomic indicator families, measures and management questions are summarized in <a href="#esp2026-tbl-socioeconomic">Table B5</a>.</p>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-economic-observations"><h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-economic-observations">Catch and Market Context</h5>
<p>The broader Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands (BSAI) pollock fishery reported 1.3163 million tons of total catch in 2024 (<a href="#esp2026-tbl-catch-exvessel-economics">Table B6</a>). Trawl catcher vessels retained 678.40 thousand tons, with an ex-vessel value of $213.43 million. These economic statistics cover the BSAI; their area and accounting definitions differ from the BS stock-assessment catch series. Published pollock-target vessel counts were 103 across harvesting sectors and 76 catcher vessels. The counts describe participation in the target fishery and include their source-specific gear definitions.</p>
<p>Published first-wholesale pollock production was 487.89 thousand tons of product weight and $1.4743 billion in 2024 (<a href="#esp2026-tbl-first-wholesale-economics">Table B7</a>). The Economic SAFE excludes confidential components from some aggregates; the combined fillet quantities and derived values for 2021–2022 remain unavailable here. Product mix and market conditions both affect the observed unit values <span class="citation">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-abelman2026economic" role="doc-biblioref">Abelman et al. 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Global Alaska pollock capture production was 3.573 million tons in 2024 (<a href="#esp2026-tbl-trade-global">Table B8</a>, panel A). The United States and Russian Federation accounted for 39.9% and 54.0%, respectively, and BSAI catch represented about 36.8% of the global total. U.S. Alaska-pollock domestic exports totaled 333 thousand tons of products valued at $1.00 billion in 2025, compared with 332 thousand tons and $0.946 billion in 2024 (panel B). These national trade statistics extend through 2025; global catch statistics extend through 2024. Their product weights, nominal export values and legacy import/destination baskets are defined in the table notes <span class="citation">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-fao2026capture" role="doc-biblioref">FAO 2026</a>; <a href="#ref-esp2026-noaa2026trade" role="doc-biblioref">NOAA Fisheries 2026</a>)</span>.</p>
<p>Among the three destination groups shown, selected European countries accounted for the largest export shares throughout 2020–2025 (<a href="#esp2026-fig-export-destinations">Figure B6</a>). Meat’s share of export volume rose from 45.8% in 2020 to 53.3% in 2025, while its value share rose from 44.0% to 53.0% (<a href="#esp2026-fig-export-product-mix">Figure B7</a>). The Russian Federation accounted for more than half of global catch in each year from 2020 to 2024 (<a href="#esp2026-fig-global-catch-origin">Figure B8</a>). First-wholesale surimi volume declined from 185.5 to 165.1 thousand tons between 2023 and 2024, while fillet volume rose from 142.9 to 158.6 thousand tons (<a href="#esp2026-fig-first-wholesale-products">Figure B9</a>).</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-annual-indicator-status">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-annual-indicator-status">Annual Indicator Status</h4>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-age-0-energy-density-through-2025">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-age-0-energy-density-through-2025">Age-0 Energy Density Through 2025</h5>
<p>The latest five available observation years are 2021–2025 (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#esp2026-tbl-energy-density">Table B9</a>). In 2025, the SEBS annual mean was 19.23 kJ/g dry mass, 0.64 lower than in 2024. The NBS annual mean was 20.84, 0.09 lower than in 2024 <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-page2026energy">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-page2026energy" role="doc-biblioref">Page and Maselko 2026</a>)</span>. These are descriptive differences between annual means. </p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-recorded-annual-indicators">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-recorded-annual-indicators">Annual Indicator Series</h5>
<p>The age-1 DSEM input spans 1964–2026 and contains 18 ecosystem series plus the assessment-derived age-1 response (<a href="#esp2026-fig-working-indicators">Figure B5</a>). Seventeen ecosystem series have 2026 values; the energy-density series ends in 2025, and age-1 observations end in 2024. </p>
<p>Standardized departures below equal each value minus that series’ mean, divided by its sample standard deviation. Each baseline uses all available finite observations, including the latest year, and retains the series’ gaps. These baselines are descriptive historical variability, rather than a common fixed climatology, sampling-error intervals or approved biological thresholds.</p>
<p>In 2026, sea ice is +0.89 SD relative to its 1985–2026 baseline of 42 observations. Cold-pool extent is +1.12 SD, SST −0.39 SD and bottom temperature −0.79 SD relative to their separate 1982–2026 baselines of 44 available observations each. Sea ice and cold pool both exceed their 2025 values. SST also increased from 2025 despite remaining below its observed-period mean, whereas bottom temperature fell.</p>
<p>The open-water bloom indicator is −1.54 SD and chlorophyll a is +0.77 SD relative to their separate 1998–2026 baselines of 29 observations each. Both declined from their 2025 values. Spring small and large copepods are −0.45 and −0.66 SD using their separate 2000–2026 baselines of 25 observations; summer small and large copepods are −0.92 and +0.21 SD using their separate 2003–2026 baselines of 22 observations. The mixed physical and prey pattern supports contextual discussion rather than an overall favorable or adverse recruitment classification.</p>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-indicator-analysis">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-indicator-analysis">Indicator Analysis</h4>
<p>The September 2026 assessment development document presents a pilot DSEM analysis of SST and cold-pool pathways (Ianelli et al. 2026). Tables B10–B11 reproduce its fit comparisons and direct proxy coefficients as an example of analyses that could be provided in the ESP.</p><section class="level5" id="esp2026-decision-support">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-decision-support">Decision Support</h5>
<p>A contextual indicator may inform the SAFE risk-table discussion when it identifies a documented condition relevant to recruitment, productivity, survey interpretation, or fishery operations. Its influence on a risk category requires an explanation of the evidence and uncertainty. A predictive indicator needs forecast evaluation and numerical checks. Incorporation into an assessment likelihood, projections, or a harvest rule requires a separate, reviewed implementation and evaluation of effects on biomass, uncertainty, ABC, and OFL.</p>
</section>
<section class="level5" id="esp2026-socioeconomic-monitoring">
<h5 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-socioeconomic-monitoring">Socioeconomic Monitoring</h5>
<p>Socioeconomic monitoring can build on the main assessment’s discussion of fishery conditions, including fishing locations, catch rates, effort, size composition, and bycatch avoidance, alongside economic performance, participation, and community exposure. The catch-decision indicators and probabilities in Tables 55 and 56 provide a framework for comparing alternative catches in terms of fishing mortality, future spawning biomass, age composition, and relative fishing pressure. The fishing-mortality-based effort proxy describes relative pressure; observed vessel effort, catchability, operating costs, and revenues would provide the economic context for interpreting it. Future ESP drafts will pursue incorporating these fishery-condition observations and decision-table comparisons to connect projected stock outcomes with operational and socioeconomic consequences.</p>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section class="level3" id="esp2026-data-gaps-and-future-research-priorities">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-data-gaps-and-future-research-priorities">Data Gaps and Future Research Priorities</h3>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-ecosystem-priorities">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-ecosystem-priorities">Ecosystem Priorities</h4>
<p> One of our priorities is cohort-aligned predator overlap or mortality, with timing that matches the survival interval. Joint juvenile and predator distributions, diet and consumption estimates, and direct fall–spring cohort comparisons would strengthen interpretation.</p>
<p>Transport and nursery delivery, prey timing and lipid content, winter exposure, and annual observation-error estimates remain additional priorities. Climate relationships should be assessed for stability across recent warm conditions and historical regimes. Long-term climate projections in Mueter et al. and Spencer et al. describe conditional scenarios <span class="citation" data-cites="esp2026-mueter2011 esp2026-spencer2016">(<a href="#ref-esp2026-mueter2011" role="doc-biblioref">Mueter et al. 2011</a>; <a href="#ref-esp2026-spencer2016" role="doc-biblioref">Spencer et al. 2016</a>)</span>; their projected effects provide research context rather than annual 2026 indicator values.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-socioeconomic-priorities">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-socioeconomic-priorities">Socioeconomic Priorities</h4>
<p>Confirm a compact pollock-specific indicator set with economic and social science contributors. Resolve sector and community definitions, annual update capacity, disclosure rules, cost comparability, and a common price base. Evaluate whether incomplete quota utilization or altered fishing patterns have identifiable operational, market, processing, or biological causes. Document the availability date for each product so the ESP distinguishes information usable during the specification process from information released later.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-completion-priorities-for-the-2026-appendix">
<h4 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-completion-priorities-for-the-2026-appendix">Completion Priorities for the 2026 Appendix</h4>
<p>Confirm the primary sources, units, seasonal and spatial definitions and observation uncertainty for the working annual series. Review the age-1 DAG and the proposed energy and predator pathways with the ESP and ecosystem teams. Preserve separate timing and scaling for the archived Rceattle pilot and standalone DSEM, and retain the AR1 forecast benchmark when evaluating any expanded model. Reconcile the historical pilot archive and its outstanding numerical checks before using the indicators to support an annual status or risk classification.</p>
</section>
<section class="level4" id="esp2026-template-completion"></section></section>
<section class="level3" id="esp2026-conclusion">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="esp2026-conclusion">Conclusion</h3>
<p>The literature supports following cohorts through spawning and delivery, prey and fall age-0 energy, first-winter survival, and later predator exposure. The ESP also considers adult productivity, survey availability and socioeconomic conditions. The regional energy-density series supplies a measured-condition indicator through 2025. </p>
<p> Economic observations extend through 2024 for the BSAI fishery and 2025 for national trade; the 2026 interpretation is qualitative.</p>
</section>

<p class="safe-apa-note" id="esp2026-tbl-trade-global-apa-note"><em>Note.</em> These observed historical statistics cover global catch and shares through 2024 and U.S. trade through 2025. Trade statistics remain revisable. Global catch is in thousand tons of live weight. Trade volumes are thousand tons of product weight. BSAI catch is a subset of U.S. catch and includes federal and state retained plus discarded catch from both the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands. Trade covers U.S.-national Alaska-pollock products across their source fisheries. Export values are nominal U.S. dollars on a free-alongside-ship (FAS) export-value basis, distinct from wholesale revenue. Unit values reflect product mix as well as market conditions. Domestic exports exclude re-exports. The legacy import basket combines Alaska and unspecified (NSPF) pollock; legacy net exports subtract that broader basket from Alaska-pollock domestic exports. The legacy statistical aggregate combines mainland China, Taiwan and Hong Kong. The selected European aggregate comprises Austria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom. It is neither the European Union nor all Europe. Meat combines Alaska-pollock products other than surimi and roe, including frozen whole/headed-and-gutted fish, fillets and other meat. Product shares sum to 100% before rounding. Values are rounded to one decimal place. Displayed net exports are rounded from the saved source totals rather than recalculated from separately rounded export and import values. Sources: NOAA Fisheries FOSS, retrieved 30 October 2026; FAO Global Capture Production release Capture_2026.1.0 (March 2026); Economic SAFE 2025, Table 4.1, p. 34, published 16 March 2026. Source links: <a href="https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/national/sustainable-fisheries/foreign-fishery-trade-data">NOAA foreign fishery trade data</a>; <a href="https://www.fao.org/fishery/en/collection/capture">FAO Global Capture Production</a>; <a href="https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/s3/2026-03/gf_safe_2026-03-16.pdf">Economic SAFE</a>.</p>

<div alt="Workshop recruitment diagram follows reproductive output through seasonal age-0 and age-1 stages to age-2 observations. Prey-quality and energetic-condition pathways connect to juvenile survival; predation indices and cold-pool extent link to later stages. Rectangular boxes identify candidate observations, and oval nodes describe population states or intermediate processes. These are preliminary hypotheses." class="quarto-float quarto-figure quarto-figure-center anchored" id="esp2026-fig-workshop-recruitment">
<figure class="quarto-float quarto-float-fig figure" data-apa-appendix-float="Figure B1"><div aria-describedby="esp2026-fig-workshop-recruitment-caption-0ceaefa1-69ba-4598-a22c-09a6ac19f8ca">
<a class="lightbox" data-gallery="esp2026-quarto-lightbox-gallery-1" href="assets/figure-075.png" title="Figure 1: Nominal seasonal catch per tow-hour for herring, sablefish, Chinook salmon, chum salmon, and pollock in EBS pollock-dominated hauls, 1991–2026. Rates equal total extrapolated catch divided by total valid tow-hours. Units are kg per tow-hour for herring and sablefish, tons per tow-hour for pollock, and fish per tow-hour for salmon. A season is January–May; B season is June–December. Hauls are in NMFS areas 500–539, with positive total catch and more than 80% pollock by weight. The 2026 B-season data extend through September 18. Missing species catches are omitted from catch sums while their tow-hours remain in the denominator; unreported species-season combinations appear as gaps. Catcher-vessel and electronic-monitoring coverage is incomplete; catcher-vessel records are absent in 2025–2026 after filtering."><img alt="Workshop recruitment diagram follows reproductive output through seasonal age-0 and age-1 stages to age-2 observations. Rectangular boxes identify candidate observations, and oval nodes describe population states or intermediate processes. These are preliminary hypotheses." aria-label="Workshop recruitment diagram follows reproductive output through seasonal age-0 and age-1 stages to age-2 observations. Prey-quality and energetic-condition pathways connect to juvenile survival; predation indices and cold-pool extent link to later stages. Rectangular boxes identify candidate observations, and oval nodes describe population states or intermediate processes. These are preliminary hypotheses." class="img-fluid figure-img" role="img" src="assets/figure-075.png" style="width:100.0%"/></a>
</div>

Shading marks provisional 2024–2025 estimates based on released FT-NIRS ages before conversion to thin-section tester ages. Both years cover all 12 months. <section class="level2 unnumbered safe-appendix-heading" id="sec-other-removals">
<h2 class="unnumbered safe-appendix-heading anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-other-removals"><span class="safe-appendix-label"><strong>Appendix C</strong></span><br/>
<span class="safe-appendix-title"><strong>Research and Other Noncommercial Pollock Removals</strong></span></h2>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="reported-noncommercial-catch">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="reported-noncommercial-catch"> Reported noncommercial catch</h3>
<p>Reported noncommercial pollock catches in the Bering Sea are summarized by collection in <a href="#app-table-b1">Table C1</a> and by year in <a href="#app-table-b2">Table C2</a>. The AKR dataset covers 1982–2025 across the Gulf of Alaska, Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands; Bering Sea records begin in 1991, with broader multisurvey coverage from 2010. These are reported collection-year amounts, rather than verified complete EBS-stock totals. Missing years and collection cells indicate absent observations. The data end in 2025.</p>
<p>The summaries use the reported Bering Sea FMP area, retaining stations from collections whose names mention other regions. Explicitly Bogoslof-named surveys are shown separately; other collections in reporting area 518 remain among the other reported Bering Sea catches. In 2024, the total was 216.280081 t, including 4.393640 t from the named Bogoslof survey and 211.886441 t from other reported Bering Sea collections. The corresponding 2025 reported total was 140.994428 t.</p>
<p>Experimental fishing permit (EFP) records account for 1,198.506090 t in 2011 and 771.516610 t in 2021. Their inclusion explains the large totals in those years. The sole 2020 record is a Bogoslof collection; other EBS research removals remain unverified for that year. Historical EFP inclusion in official catch accounting requires reconciliation. AKR metadata state that no 2025 EFP catches occurred outside CAS.</p>
<p>Weights are converted from kilograms to tons using the units corroborated by <a href="https://mail.google.com/mail/u/?authuser=jim.ianelli%40noaa.gov#all/1a13617188c1ece3">AKR dataset correspondence</a>, dated 9 October and forwarded on 13 October 2026. Annual completeness of the AKR dataset received on 27 October remains unverified. The 2020–2023 totals agree, after rounding, with the accepted 2024 SAFE’s research-catch table <span class="citation" data-cites="ianelli2024safe">(<a href="#ref-ianelli2024safe" role="doc-biblioref">Ianelli et al. 2024</a>)</span>. Noncommercial removals are reported separately from assessment catch. The full annual summaries and source record retain the collection details and reporting qualifications.</p>
</section>
<section class="level3 unnumbered" id="exempted-fishing-and-other-removal-categories">
<h3 class="unnumbered anchored" data-anchor-id="exempted-fishing-and-other-removal-categories"> Exempted fishing and other removal categories</h3>
<p>The 2025 EFP 2025-01 permit and 2026 renewal allow up to <strong>3,000 t of total groundfish</strong>, rather than pollock alone, to be exempt from TAC during each permit’s effective period; additional groundfish catch counts against TAC. This authorization ceiling is separate from observed removals. Actual pollock catch under these permits and its accounting treatment require permit-specific records.</p>
<p>EFP 2024-02 provides a footrope/gear exemption and otherwise retains applicable regulations. It supplies no basis for assuming a TAC exemption. The noncommercial dataset includes BS-labelled subsistence records in 1991 and 1994; complete recent stock-specific subsistence, recreational and other-FMP removals remain unverified.</p>
</section>

Recruitment and selectivity deviations are expressed on their fitted deviation or increment scales; the biological and selectivity schedules show their realized effects. The full precision data also supply natural-scale transformations where applicable.</p>

<section class="level2 unnumbered safe-appendix-heading" id="sec-proposed-projection-input-curves">
<h2 class="unnumbered safe-appendix-heading anchored" data-anchor-id="sec-proposed-projection-input-curves"><span class="safe-appendix-label"><strong>Appendix E</strong></span><br/>
<span class="safe-appendix-title"><strong>Proposed Projection Input Curves</strong></span></h2>
<p>The proposed three-year fishery-selectivity average is compared with the window including the inferred 2026 curve (<a class="quarto-xref" href="#fig-proposed-tier3-selectivity">Figure E1</a>). The technical appendix records their conditional projection effects.</p>
<div alt="Fishery selectivity at ages 1 to 15 plus compares the proposed 2023 to 2025 average with a 2024 to 2026 average. Solid-circle and dashed-triangle curves distinguish the two selected averaging windows. Colour, line type and point shape distinguish the curves." class="quarto-float quarto-figure quarto-figure-center anchored" id="fig-proposed-tier3-selectivity">
<figure class="quarto-float quarto-float-fig figure" data-apa-appendix-float="Figure E1"><div aria-describedby="fig-proposed-tier3-selectivity-caption-0ceaefa1-69ba-4598-a22c-09a6ac19f8ca">
<a class="lightbox" data-gallery="quarto-lightbox-gallery-73" href="assets/figure-086.png" title="Figure 73: Annual Model 26.0 fishery selectivity and fully selected F35%, a proxy for FMSY, for 2001–2026. Mean selected age uses ages 1–10; SPR uses ages 1–14 and 15+, fixed mortality, maturity and the selected projection spawning weights, and quarter-year spawning timing. Curves are normalized to maximum one. The 2024 figure plotted FMSY."><img alt="Fishery selectivity at ages 1 to 15 plus compares the proposed 2023 to 2025 average with a 2024 to 2026 average. Solid-circle and dashed-triangle curves distinguish the two selected averaging windows. Colour, line type and point shape distinguish the curves." aria-label="Fishery selectivity at ages 1 to 15 plus compares the proposed 2023 to 2025 average with a 2024 to 2026 average. Solid-circle and dashed-triangle curves distinguish the two selected averaging windows. Colour, line type and point shape distinguish the curves." class="img-fluid figure-img" role="img" src="assets/figure-086.png"/></a>
</div>
<p class="safe-apa-note" id="fig-proposed-tier3-selectivity-apa-note"><em>Note.</em> Proposed three-year fishery selectivity and the alternative window check. The two curves are distinguished by colour, line type and point shape.</p>
<figcaption class="safe-apa-caption safe-caption safe-caption-apa safe-caption-hanging" data-safe-caption-layout="label-hanging-text" id="fig-proposed-tier3-selectivity-caption-0ceaefa1-69ba-4598-a22c-09a6ac19f8ca"><span class="safe-caption-label">Figure E1 </span><span class="safe-caption-text">Proposed Fishery Selectivity and Alternative Averaging Window</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</div>
<p>The projection uses the fixed 2027 fishery forecast for both catch and spawning weights, alongside the population-weight schedule (<a href="#fig-proposed-tier3-weights">Figure E2</a>).</p>
<div alt="Four curves show weight in kilograms by age. The projected fishery schedule differs from 2026 weights, particularly at younger selected ages. Population and spawning weights are held at 2026 levels. Colour, line type and point shape distinguish schedules." class="quarto-float quarto-figure quarto-figure-center anchored" id="fig-proposed-tier3-weights">
<figure class="quarto-float quarto-float-fig figure" data-apa-appendix-float="Figure E2"><div aria-describedby="fig-proposed-tier3-weights-caption-0ceaefa1-69ba-4598-a22c-09a6ac19f8ca">

Colour, line type and point shape distinguish schedules." aria-label="Four curves show weight in kilograms by age. The projected fishery schedule differs from 2026 weights, particularly at younger selected ages. Population and spawning weights are held at 2026 levels. Colour, line type and point shape distinguish schedules." class="img-fluid figure-img" role="img" src="assets/figure-087.png"/></a>
</div>
